# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L579-L632


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `liquidatePositionBadDebt` function in the `CDPVault` contract incorrectly updates the quota revenue based on the total debt instead of the actual repaid amount. Thiss leads to inaccurate accounting of quota revenue

## Proof of Concept
In the [`liquidatePositionBadDebt`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L579-L632) function, the `loss` is calculated as the difference between the total debt and the repay amount:

```solidity
uint256 loss = calcTotalDebt(debtData) - repayAmount;
```

The function then calls `pool.repayCreditAccount` with the total debt and zero profit:

```solidity
pool.repayCreditAccount(debtData.debt, 0, loss); // U:[CM-11]
```

But when updating the quota revenue, it incorrectly considers the total debt instead of the actual repaid amount:

```solidity
int256 quotaRevenueChange = _calcQuotaRevenueChange(-int(debtData.debt));
if (quotaRevenueChange != 0) {
    IPoolV3(pool).updateQuotaRevenue(quotaRevenueChange); // U:[PQK-15]
}
```

This means that the quota revenue is updated based on the total debt, even though a portion of that debt was not actually repaid due to the bad debt (`loss`). This can lead to an overestimation of the quota revenue.


## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The `quotaRevenueChange` should be calculated based on the actual repaid amount (`repayAmount`) instead of the total debt. 

```diff
function liquidatePositionBadDebt(address owner, uint256 repayAmount) external whenNotPaused {
   
......

    pool.repayCreditAccount(debtData.debt, 0, loss); // U:[CM-11]
    // transfer the collateral amount from the vault to the liquidator
    token.safeTransfer(msg.sender, takeCollateral);

-   int256 quotaRevenueChange = _calcQuotaRevenueChange(-int(debtData.debt));
+   int256 quotaRevenueChange = _calcQuotaRevenueChange(-int(repayAmount));
    if (quotaRevenueChange != 0) {
        IPoolV3(pool).updateQuotaRevenue(quotaRevenueChange); // U:[PQK-15]
    }
}
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L598-L608


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The implementation of `liquidatePositionBadDebt` function does not allow for partial liquidations of positions with bad debt. This limitation can discourage liquidators from acting on large positions leading to the accumulation of bad debt in the system. 

## Proof of Concept
Take a look at the `liquidatePositionBadDebt` function, where the logic forces the liquidation of the entire position regardless of the `repayAmount` provided by the liquidator.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L598-L608
```solidity
598:         // Enusure that the debt is greater than the collateral at discounted price
599:         if (calcTotalDebt(debtData) <= wmul(position.collateral, discountedPrice)) revert CDPVault__noBadDebt();
600:         // compute collateral to take, debt to repay
601:         uint256 takeCollateral = wdiv(repayAmount, discountedPrice);
602:         if (takeCollateral < position.collateral) revert CDPVault__repayAmountNotEnough();
603: 
604:         // account for bad debt
605:         takeCollateral = position.collateral;
606:         repayAmount = wmul(takeCollateral, discountedPrice);
607:         uint256 loss = calcTotalDebt(debtData) - repayAmount;
```

On line 599, the function first checks if the total debt exceeds the discounted value of the collateral. If not, it reverts with `CDPVault__noBadDebt`.

On 601, it then calculates the amount of collateral (`takeCollateral`) that the provided `repayAmount` would cover.

If this amount is less than the total collateral, it reverts with `CDPVault__repayAmountNotEnough` as seen on 602.

However, immediately after this check, it sets `takeCollateral` to the full amount of collateral in the position thereby totally ignoring the initial calculation.

This means that even if a liquidator only wants to repay a portion of the bad debt, they will always end up liquidating the entire position.

## Tools used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Modify the function to consistently use the original `repayAmount` provided by the liquidator, allowing for partial liquidations of bad debt positions.


## Assessed type

Context

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
PoolV3's interest rate will be off if a credit account is repaid with profit because it doesn't consider the expected liquidity increase.
 
## Proof of Concept
When a credit account is repaid it can either incur a loss or a profit for the pool. In case of a loss, the expected liquidity is decreased by that amount to reflect the loss in the interest calculation. The same thing has to be done in case of a profit.

```sol
    function repayCreditAccount(
        uint256 repaidAmount,
        uint256 profit,
        uint256 loss
    )
        external
        override
        creditManagerOnly // U:[LP-2C]
        whenNotPaused // U:[LP-2A]
        nonReentrant // U:[LP-2B]
    {
        // ...

        _updateBaseInterest({
            expectedLiquidityDelta: -loss.toInt256(),
            availableLiquidityDelta: 0,
            checkOptimalBorrowing: false
        }); // U:[LP-14B,14C,14D]
        // ...
    }
```

It only subtracts the loss. It never adds the profit to the expected liquidity.

See the original Gearbox contract for the correct implementation: https://github.com/Gearbox-protocol/core-v3/blob/main/contracts/pool/PoolV3.sol#L503

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/PoolV3.sol#L330
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/PoolV3.sol#L306


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
PoolV3 takes a fee on every withdrawal. Because it uses two different formulas to calculate the fee in `withdraw()` and `redeem()` it's slightly cheaper to use `redeem()`.

## Proof of Concept
`withdraw()` calculates the amount of shares to burn using `_amountWithWithdrawalFee()`:

```sol
    function _amountWithWithdrawalFee(uint256 amount) internal view returns (uint256) {
        return (amount * PERCENTAGE_FACTOR) / (PERCENTAGE_FACTOR - withdrawFee);
    }
```

While `redeem()` calculates the amount of assets the user receives using `_amountMinusWithdrawalFee()`:

```sol
   function _amountMinusWithdrawalFee(uint256 amount) internal view returns (uint256) {
        return (amount * (PERCENTAGE_FACTOR - withdrawFee)) / PERCENTAGE_FACTOR;
    }
```

Given that `PERCENTAGE_FACTOR = 10,000`, `withdrawFee = 100`, and assets and shares being redeemable 1:1:

user calls `withdraw()` with 1e18:

$shares = 1e18 * 10,000 / 9,900 = 1.010101e18$

Same thing but the user redeems 1e18 shares:

$assets = 1e18 * 9,900 / 10,000 = 9.9e17$

In `redeem()` you pay $1e18 - 9.9e17 = 1e16 assets$ in fees. In `withdraw()` you pay $1.010101e18 - 1e18 = 1.010101e16 assets$ in fees.

## Tools Used
none

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Changr `_amountWithWithdrawalFee()` to:

```sol
    function _amountWithWithdrawalFee(uint256 amount) internal view returns (uint256) {
        return amount + amount * withdrawFee / PERCENTAGE_FACTOR;
    }
```


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L509-L633


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Detail
The `liquidatePosition` and `liquidatePositionBadDebt` functions in `CDPVault.sol` revert when the spot price is zero, effectively pausing liquidations. However, when the spot price becomes non-zero again, there's no grace period before liquidations can resume. This can lead to immediate liquidations of positions that became undercollateralized during the price feed outage, unfairly disadvantaging users.

## Impact
This vulnerability can have severe consequences:

- Unfair Liquidations: Users whose positions became undercollateralized during the price feed outage can be liquidated immediately when the feed resumes, without a chance to adjust their positions.
- Advantage to Liquidation Bots: Liquidation bots can exploit this situation, liquidating positions before users have a chance to react.
- User Losses: Users may suffer unnecessary losses due to inability to manage their positions during and immediately after the oracle failure.

## Proof of Concept
In the CDPVault contract:
```
// File: CDPVault.sol
// Lines 522-524 (liquidatePosition function)
uint256 spotPrice_ = spotPrice();
if (spotPrice_ == 0) revert CDPVault__liquidatePosition_invalidSpotPrice();

// Lines 590-591 (liquidatePositionBadDebt function)
uint256 spotPrice_ = spotPrice();
if (spotPrice_ == 0) revert CDPVault__liquidatePosition_invalidSpotPrice();
```

These checks prevent liquidations when the price is zero but offer no protection immediately after the price becomes non-zero.

## Tools Used
Manual code review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a grace time after the price becomes non-zero, such that liquidations can only be executed after the grace time has passed, giving enough time for users to adjust their margins.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/quotas/GaugeV3.sol#L78-L92


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Detail
The `GaugeV3` contract, which is responsible for managing quota rates based on user votes, contains an issue in its epoch update mechanism. The problem lies in the `_checkAndUpdateEpoch` function, which is called by various operations including voting and unvoting.

The current implementation of `_checkAndUpdateEpoch` is as follows:
```
function _checkAndUpdateEpoch() internal {
    uint16 epochNow = IGearStakingV3(voter).getCurrentEpoch(); // U:[GA-14]

    if (epochNow > epochLastUpdate) {
        epochLastUpdate = epochNow; // U:[GA-14]

        if (!epochFrozen) {
            // The quota keeper should call back to retrieve quota rates for needed tokens
            _poolQuotaKeeper().updateRates(); // U:[GA-14]
        }

        emit UpdateEpoch(epochNow); // U:[GA-14]
    }
}
```
The issue arises from the fact that `epochLastUpdate` is always updated to the current epoch, regardless of whether the contract is in a frozen state or not. However, the actual rate update (via `_poolQuotaKeeper().updateRates()`) only occurs when the contract is not frozen.
This creates a discrepancy between the recorded last update epoch and the actual last rate update, which becomes problematic when the contract transitions from a frozen to an unfrozen state.

The current implementation allows voting to continue during frozen periods, but doesn't update rates, leading to a discrepancy between voting activity and actual rate adjustments.
## Impact
- Outdated Rates: During frozen periods and immediately after unfreezing, the system operates with outdated rates that don't reflect current voting state.
- Economic Implications: Users interacting with the system during these periods may be unfairly advantaged or disadvantaged based on outdated rates.
- Compressed Rate Updates: When unfreezing, multiple epochs of voting are compressed into a single rate update, potentially causing abrupt and significant rate changes.

## Proof of Concept
Scenario demonstrating the issue:

- GaugeV3 is operational at epoch 100 with current rates.
- The contract is frozen at epoch 101.
- Users continue voting during epochs 102-106, but rates remain unchanged.
- The contract is unfrozen at the start of epoch 107.
- _checkAndUpdateEpoch is called:
    It updates epochLastUpdate to 107.
    It triggers a rate update.
    This update compresses all voting activity from epochs 101-106 into a single rate change.
- Users interacting with the system during epochs 101-107 are subject to outdated rates, and the sudden rate change at 107 may cause unexpected economic impacts.

## Tools Used
Manual code review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
- Block voting and unvoting during frozen periods
- Implement a grace period after unfreezing


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L109


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details 
To withdraw lpETH from StakingLPEth contract, users have to first call `cooldownAssets`. This will update the user's `cooldownEnd` and `underlyingAmount`. 

If `cooldownAssets` is called again by the same user in-between `cooldownEnd` and the current time, then it will increase `underlyingAmount` AND increase the `cooldownEnd` for all the funds, not just the newly cooldown funds. 

Consider the following scenario
1. A user calls `cooldownAssets` for 10 lpETH, this updates `underlyingAmount = 10` AND `cooldownEnd = block.timestamp + 30 days`
2. After 25 days the same user wants to unlock their remaining lpETH so they call `cooldownAssets` for 15 lpETH, this updates `underlyingAmount = 25` AND `cooldownEnd = block.timestamp + 30 days`

The issue is that the new cooldown has applied for the OLD 10 lpETH that was already cooling down for 25 days

## Impact
Users will have funds locked for longer than expected

In the worst case this leads to a 30 day DOS

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. Create a mapping that maps every user to a size 10 array of UserCooldown structs

```solidity
mapping(address => UserCooldown[10]) public userCooldowns;
```

2. When a user calls `cooldownAssets`, populate a slot in userCooldowns[msg.sender]

3. When a user withdraws iterate over each element of userCooldowns[msg.sender], and for each slot that `if (block.timestamp >= userCooldown.cooldownEnd `, allow them to withdraw the lpETH






## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L28


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details 
The `StakingLPEth` contract is an ERC4626 vault. To prevent the well known inflation attack the protocol has implemented a `MIN_SHARES = 0.01 ether`. 

After every deposit/withdraw, there is a `_checkMinShares()` function to ensure the minimum number of shares is >= 0.01 ether. 

The issue is that 0.01 ether is a significant amount of funds to lock in the contract. It can lead to the following fund loss/DOS scenario

1. User A deposits 1 lpETH
2. User B deposits 0.005 lpETH (~$20)
3. User C deposits 0.005 lpETH (~$20)
4. User A withdraws 1 lpETH
5. User B/C withdraw attempts will revert indefinitely 

Simply using MIN_SHARES = 1000, which is a dust amount, is enough to make the inflation attack 1000x more expensive for the attacker i.e. to steal 1 ETH the attacker will lose 1000 ETH, while locking up only a dust amount.

## Impact
Users can have lost funds up to 0.01 lpETH

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Very simple solution

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details 
In the `CDPVault` contract the `deposit` and `withdraw` functions are meant to revert when the protocol is paused, this is because they have the `whenNotPaused` modifier.

The purpose of the deposit/withdraw functions is to slightly manipulate the user input params and pass them into `modifyCollateralAndDebt()` function to actually change the state.

The issue is that an attacker can easily bypass this by directly calling the public `modifyCollateralAndDebt` function with the appropriate params for a deposit/withdraw. Since this function does not have the `whenNotPaused` modifier, the Tx will go through even if the protocol is paused.

## Impact
Attacker can deposit/withdraw through `modifyCollateralAndDebt` when the protocol is paused.

If there is an exploit involving the depositing/withdrawing, pausing the protocol will not stop the attacker.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
There are a few solutions

1. Make `modifyCollateralAndDebt()` an internal function
2. If `modifyCollateralAndDebt()` must remain public, revert if paused when `(deltaCollateral > 0 || deltaCollateral < 0)`

Make sure repayments are not paused else borrowers will unfairly accumulate interest and may be quickly liquidated by a bot once unpaused

## Vulnerability Details 
Chainlink aggregators have a built-in circuit breaker if the price of an asset goes outside of a predetermined price band. The result is that if an asset experiences a huge drop in value (i.e. LUNA crash) the price of the oracle will continue to return the minPrice instead of the actual price of the asset.

This would allow user to continue borrowing with the asset but at the wrong price, which will lead to draining of the protocol. This is exactly what happened to [Venus](https://rekt.news/venus-blizz-rekt/) on BSC when LUNA imploded. However, the protocol missed to implement such a check.

It is medium severity because the likelihood of such an event to drop the price of the asset below the minimum is low

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
get the minPrice and maxPrice from the aggregator, then compare it to the price. revert if it is outside the bounds

```solidity
IERC20(asset()).safeApprove(rewardPool, assets);
```

This causes a permanent DOS of these functions in the AuraVault `deposit()`, `mint()` and `claim()`. Rendering the contract useless.

Complete DOS of `deposit()`, `mint()` and `claim()` functions, rendering the contract useless

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
use the `forceApprove` function instead

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/reward/ChefIncentivesController.sol#L627


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details 
The `ChefIncentivesController` contract offers two approaches for reward distribution:

1. A fixed `rewardsPerSecond` value
2. A dynamic `rewardsPerSecond` value based on an emission schedule

For the emission schedule method, regular checks are necessary to compare the current rewards per second against the schedule, determining when adjustments are needed. This functionality is implemented in the `setScheduledRewardsPerSecond` function, which is called by `_updateEmissions`.

However, an inconsistency exists in the current implementation. The `_updateEmissions` function is only utilized in `addPool` and `claim` operations. It is notably absent in `_handleActionAfterForToken` and `afterLockUpdate`. These functions call `_updatePool` to recalculate pool rewards using `rewardsPerSecond`, but they don't account for potential changes in the emission schedule.

This oversight could result in inaccurate reward emissions until either a new pool is added or a claim is processed. To address this issue, it's advisable to invoke `_updateEmissions` whenever reward recalculations are necessary. This approach would ensure that the `rewardsPerSecond` value consistently aligns with the current scheduled emission rate, maintaining accuracy in reward distribution across all relevant contract functions.

## Impact
Rewards distributed to users may be inaccurate, potentially leading to over- or under-payment of incentives. This discrepancy could persist until `addPool` is called or a claim is processed, potentially affecting the fairness of the reward system and the economic balance of the protocol.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To mitigate this issue, call _updateEmissions in all functions that update rewards, ensuring consistent alignment with the current emission schedule.

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details 
In the repayCreditAccount function of the PoolV3 contract, there is an inconsistency in the calculation of the expectedLiquidityDelta parameter passed to the _updateBaseInterest function:

```solidity 
_updateBaseInterest({
            expectedLiquidityDelta: -loss.toInt256(), //@audit should be profit - loss
            availableLiquidityDelta: 0,
            checkOptimalBorrowing: false
        }); // U:[LP-14B,14C,14D]
```

The issue is that this calculation only considers the loss value, ignoring the profit parameter entirely.

Since the profit will impact interest rate calculations it should be included in this function

## Impact
The major impact is:

Inaccurate Interest Rate Adjustments: The miscalculation of expectedLiquidityDelta leads to incorrect updates of the base interest rate. This could result in the protocol either undercharging or overcharging interest on loans, potentially causing significant financial imbalances over time.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update the expectedLiquidityDelta calculation to account for both profit and loss:

```solidity
_updateBaseInterest({
            expectedLiquidityDelta: profit.toInt256() - loss.toInt256(),
            availableLiquidityDelta: 0,
            checkOptimalBorrowing: false
        }); // U:[LP-14B,14C,14D]
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L535


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Chainlink aggregators have a built in circuit breaker if the price of an asset goes outside of a predetermined price range. The result is that if an asset experiences a flash crash in value, the price that the oracle returns will be the minPrice instead of the actual price of the asset. An example of such a scenario would be the LUNA crash.

The _fetchAndValidate() function in ChainlinkOracle.sol does not check if the priced returned is equal to the min or max price. In such cases the actual market price of the asset could be less/more than the price returned from the Chainlink Oracle. The internal function _fetchAndValidate() is used by the external spot() function to fetch the price of a token using a Chainlink Oracle. This external spot() function is used by the CDPVault::spotPrice() function to get the current spot price of the collateral token. This spotPrice is used to calculate the collateral value to check if an account is properly collateralized when borrowing or withdrawing. 

During a flash crash where the price dips below the minPrice, users will be able to borrow or withdrawal even when they should not be able to do so because their collateral value will be calculated at the Oracle's minPrice rather than the lower actual market price. 

The spotPrice() value is also used in the liquidatePosition() function, so in the case of a flash crash mentioned above, users who should be liquidated will not be done so due to their inaccurate and inflated collateral values. 

This was the underlying cause behind the Venus Protocol and Blizz Finance drainings : https://rekt.news/venus-blizz-rekt/

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
ChainlinkOracle.sol should have a check to make sure that the answer is in the valid price range. Something like :
```
if (answer >= maxPrice or answer <= minPrice){
    isValid = false;
```

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/PoolV3.sol#L529


# Vulnerability details

## Summary

The `repayCreditAccount` function in the PoolV3 contract assumes that the required amount (repaidAmount + profit + loss) has been correctly transferred to the pool without performing an internal verification. This omission can lead to significant financial discrepancies, including underfunded pool states, incorrect financial accounting, potential exploits, loss to the treasury, and ultimately, the erosion of protocol


## Impact
The insufficient verification of token transfers in the `repayCreditAccount` function can lead to several critical issues that impact the integrity, stability, and reliability of the pool, as well as the broader protocol. Here are the key impacts:

1. Underfunded Pool
If the repaidAmount, profit, and loss are not fully covered by the transferred tokens, the pool's actual liquidity becomes less than what the internal records state. This underfunded state can severely impact the pool's ability to meet future obligations.
Consequence: Liquidity providers may face withdrawal issues as the pool may not have enough tokens to honor redemption requests. This can lead to a loss of trust in the protocol.
2. Incorrect Financial Accounting
The function updates the pool’s internal state, minting or burning shares and adjusting debt parameters based on the assumption that the correct amount has been transferred. With insufficient transfers, the state is updated incorrectly.
Consequence: This can lead to misleading financial data, where the protocol’s metrics and health indicators do not reflect the true state of liquidity and debts. It can mask underlying issues until they manifest in more severe failures.
3. Potential Exploits
Malicious actors can exploit this vulnerability to deliberately underfund the pool while making it appear as though debts have been repaid. This can be especially critical if coordinated across multiple accounts.
Consequence: Attackers can drain the pool's resources, leading to financial losses for legitimate users and potentially collapsing the pool's structure.
4. Loss to Treasury
In cases where profit is specified but not actually transferred, the protocol mints new shares to the treasury based on non-existent profits, leading to inflation of shares without corresponding value.
Consequence: This could devalue the shares held by other users and disrupt the expected returns for liquidity providers.

## Proof of Concept
Demonstrate how the `repayCreditAccount` function can be called without transferring the required amount of tokens, leading to potential financial discrepancies.

Scenario Outline
Initial Setup:
Assume a credit manager has previously borrowed from the pool.
The credit manager attempts to repay part of the debt without transferring sufficient tokens to the pool address.

Key Insight
The `repayCreditAccount` function does not internally check whether the amount needed has actually been transferred to the pool's address before adjusting the pool's state and debt parameters.

Concrete Example
Variables:

repaidAmount = 300 ether
profit = 400 ether
loss = 100 ether
totalNeeded = repaidAmount + profit + loss = 800 ether
Attempt Repayment with Insufficient Tokens:

Assume the credit manager transfers only 100 ether to the pool.

The `repayCreditAccount` function processes the repayment without verifying the total transferred amount:

```solidity

function repayCreditAccount(
        uint256 repaidAmount,
        uint256 profit,
        uint256 loss
    )
        external
        override
        creditManagerOnly // U:[LP-2C]
        whenNotPaused // U:[LP-2A]
        nonReentrant // U:[LP-2B]
    {
        uint128 repaidAmountU128 = repaidAmount.toUint128();

        DebtParams storage cmDebt = _creditManagerDebt[msg.sender];
        uint128 cmBorrowed = cmDebt.borrowed;
        if (cmBorrowed == 0) {
            revert CallerNotCreditManagerException(); // U:[LP-2C,14A]
        }

        if (profit > 0) {
            _mint(treasury, convertToShares(profit)); // U:[LP-14B]
        } else if (loss > 0) {
            address treasury_ = treasury;
            uint256 sharesInTreasury = balanceOf(treasury_);
            uint256 sharesToBurn = convertToShares(loss);
            if (sharesToBurn > sharesInTreasury) {
                unchecked {
                    emit IncurUncoveredLoss({
                        creditManager: msg.sender,
                        loss: convertToAssets(sharesToBurn - sharesInTreasury)
                    }); // U:[LP-14D]
                }
                sharesToBurn = sharesInTreasury;
            }
            _burn(treasury_, sharesToBurn); // U:[LP-14C,14D]
        }

        _updateBaseInterest({
            expectedLiquidityDelta: -loss.toInt256(),
            availableLiquidityDelta: 0,
            checkOptimalBorrowing: false
        }); // U:[LP-14B,14C,14D]

        _totalDebt.borrowed -= repaidAmountU128; // U:[LP-14B,14C,14D]
        cmDebt.borrowed = cmBorrowed - repaidAmountU128; // U:[LP-14B,14C,14D]

        emit Repay(msg.sender, repaidAmount, profit, loss); // U:[LP-14B,14C,14D]
    }

```
Result
Expected Behavior: The function assumes that 800 ether has been transferred.
Actual Outcome: Only 100 ether was transferred, but the function proceeds, causing an inconsistency in the pool's accounting.


## Tools Used

Foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Implement a verification step within the repayCreditAccount function to ensure that the required amount (repaidAmount + profit + loss) has been transferred to the pool before proceeding with updates.


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Vulnerability details

<https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/PoolV3.sol#L427-L439>

PoolV3 use `_convertToShares()` for most operation.

Here is use `convertToShares()`.

```solidity
    /** @dev See {IERC4626-convertToShares}. */
    function convertToShares(uint256 assets) public view virtual override returns (uint256) {
        return _convertToShares(assets, Math.Rounding.Down);
    }

    /** @dev See {IERC4626-convertToAssets}. */
    function convertToAssets(uint256 shares) public view virtual override returns (uint256) {
        return _convertToAssets(shares, Math.Rounding.Down);
    }
```

`PoolV3` never override `_convertToAssets(uint256, Math.Rounding)`.
So it use default ERC4626 conversion logic: share = inputAssets * totalSupply / totalAssets.

Because assets here will be lended away. so conversion ratio rarely 1:1. Causing conversion error.

The end results would be treasury profit/loss recording might be different from expected.

Fix Typo, `convertToShares()` to `_convertToShares()`

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L109
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L122


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When a user initiates a partial redeem or withdrawal of their staked assets using the ``cooldownAssets`` or ``cooldownShares`` functions, the cooldown period is reset for all of the user's initialized redeem/withdrawal requests. If the user makes a subsequent request to redeem or withdraw additional assets before the initial cooldown period expires, the cooldown timer is reset for the entire amount. This causes an unintended extension of the cooldown period for the assets originally requested, forcing users to wait longer than expected to access their funds.
This could lead to frustration and potential financial inconvenience for users who need timely access to their assets.

## Proof of Concept
1) ## Initial Setup
- User A has 100 tokens staked.
- User A initiates a withdraw process for 50 tokens by calling ``cooldownAssets(50)`` at timestamp 10.
- The cooldown duration is 10, so the tokens should be available at timestamp 20.

2) ## Scenario
- Before the cooldown ends, at timestamp 15, User A decides to withdraw the remaining 50 tokens by calling ``cooldownAssets(50)`` again.

3) ## Unexpected Behavior
- Instead of allowing the first 50 tokens to be redeemable at timestamp 20, the cooldown for all 100 tokens is reset, causing the cooldown to end at timestamp 25 for both requests.
- User A now has to wait an additional 5 timestamp periods for the initial 50 tokens that should have been available at timestamp 20.

## Tools Used
manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Try separate each redeem/withdrawal request using mappings


## Assessed type

Timing

raw_row.title: The last user to withdraw will be DOS and unexpectedly revert due to the _checkMinShares in the StakingLPEth contract.

title: The last user to withdraw will be DOS and unexpectedly revert due to the _checkMinShares in the StakingLPEth contract.
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/4f508781a49ffa53511e7e5ed6cda0ff0eb5bdc5/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L28-L28


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
User who withdraws last will be DOS and his funds will be locked.
Initially when shares are worth 1:1 with assets shares locked is about $32 dollars worth but this is subject to increase as the share value increases. Suppose if in the future with more rewards coming in shares are now worth 1:2 i.e. 1 share = 2 assets then the user's loss will also double in value, as can also be seen from [docs](https://docs.loopfi.xyz/the-protocol/lending-passive-eth-yield#:~:text=At%20launch%20the%20value%20will%20be%201%20slpETH%20%3D%201%20lpETH%2C%20but%20slpETH%20is%20expected%20to%20slowly%20increase%20in%20value%20as%20protocol%20yield%20is%20transferred%20into%20the%20Staking%20smart%20contract.). 

## Proof of Concept
Whenever withdraw is called, it checks for min shares 
```javascript
    function _withdraw(
        address caller,
        address receiver,
        address _owner,
        uint256 assets,
        uint256 shares
    ) internal override nonReentrant {
        super._withdraw(caller, receiver, _owner, assets, shares);
        _checkMinShares();
    }
```
```javascript
    function _checkMinShares() internal view {
        uint256 _totalSupply = totalSupply();
        if (_totalSupply > 0 && _totalSupply < MIN_SHARES) revert MinSharesViolation();
    }
```
and min shares is ```0.01e18``` ;
```javascript
uint256 private constant MIN_SHARES = 0.01 ether;
```
The problem here is that there can be leftover dust which is not owned by a withdrawer which can DOS his transaction due to how the ```_chekMinShares``` works:
```if (_totalSupply > 0 && _totalSupply < MIN_SHARES) revert MinSharesViolation();```.

There are two ways in which the last withdrawer can be DOS, 
* unintentionally accumulated dust amount of shares due to roundings when other users withdraw, OR
* intentionally by a malicious actor by leaving just 1(dust amount) of shares when he withdraws his shares.

Example-
* there are five users with 10e18 shares each 
* first four user has withdrawn, leaving 1(dust) amount of shares 
* now 10e18 + 1 shares are left i.e. ```totalSupply() = 10e18 + 1```
* last user(Bob) tries to withdraw and calls redeem with 10e18 but it will revert because of ```_checkMinShares```,
```if (_totalSupply > 0 && _totalSupply < MIN_SHARES) revert MinSharesViolation();``` and bob cannot withdraw all because of that 1 dust leftover: ```1 > 0 && 1 < 0.01eth``` so it reverts.

Only way Bob can withdraw is to abandon his 0.01e18 shares which is worth around $32 dollars currently.
The problem is ```0.01 ether``` as ```MIN_SHARES``` is too much since we are dealing with an eth derivative token and 0.01 eth lost by a user is not a negligible amount. 

## Tools Used
manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
reduce the amount of min shares required
```diff
-      uint256 private constant MIN_SHARES = 0.01 ether;
+      uint256 private constant MIN_SHARES = 1000;
```
Just this 1000(dust) is enough to make the attack ```1000 times``` more expensive i.e. to grief ```1 LPEth``` of a user the attacker has to donate more than ```1000 LPEth``` and besides even if he continues to do so, the openzeppelin's ```_decimalsOffset``` will make the attacker lose half of his donation.

This doesn't completely solve the problem but Bob(last withdrawer) will only loss 1000(dust) shares worth $0 dollars, which is negligible. But Bob's transaction will still be unexpectedly reverted the first time and Bob will have to figure out on his own how to overcome his problem(which is to abandon 1000(dust) of his shares).  


OR 

Another suggestion would be to completely remove the additional ```_checkMinShares``` protection, because the ```decimalsOffset``` alone is enough to make the attack unprofitable and lock the attackers assets. 
And require that we mint atleast 1 share everytime someone deposits 
```diff
    function _deposit(address caller, address receiver, uint256 assets, uint256 shares) internal override nonReentrant {
+       require( shares > 0, "mint atleast 1 share");
        super._deposit(caller, receiver, assets, shares);
        _checkMinShares();
    }
```





## Assessed type

Decimal

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L428


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `liquidatePosition` function includes a call to `pool.repayCreditAccount`, an external function in another contract. External calls like this can fail for various reasons, including gas limits, contract bugs, or intentional reverts. However, the current implementation of liquidatePosition does not check whether the repayCreditAccount call was successful.

If the external call fails and the function does not handle the failure, the vault may incorrectly assume that the debt has been repaid when it has not. This can lead to an inconsistent state where the vault’s records do not match the actual debt levels, potentially causing financial discrepancies.
```
pool.repayCreditAccount(debtData.debt - newDebt, profit, 0);
```
The `liquidatePosition` function calls `pool.repayCreditAccount` to process the debt repayment during liquidation. The function then proceeds with other operations, assuming that the repayment was successful.

## Proof of Concept
An attacker could create a pool contract that always fails the `repayCreditAccount` call. When `liquidatePosition` is executed, the vault would mistakenly believe that the debt has been repaid, leading to an incorrect state.

```
contract MaliciousPool {
    function repayCreditAccount(uint256, uint256, uint256) external pure returns (bool) {
        return false; // Always fail
    }
}
```

Replace the pool contract in the `CDPVault` with the `MaliciousPool` that always fails the `repayCreditAccount` call.
Trigger the `liquidatePosition` function with a liquidation scenario.
Observe that the vault does not handle the failure and assumes the debt was repaid.

Impact:

Incorrect Debt Repayment Tracking: If the debt is not properly repaid but the vault believes it has been, this could lead to incorrect debt balances and potential insolvency risks.
Operational Issues: Over time, unhandled failures could lead to systemic issues in debt management within the vault, potentially affecting all users.
Security Risks: Attackers could exploit this vulnerability to manipulate debt positions, potentially leading to financial losses.

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `flashLoan` and `creditFlashLoan` functions in `Flashlender.sol` calculate the fee using the following formula:
```
uint256 fee = wmul(amount, protocolFee);
```
This code calculates the fee based on the amount and `protocolFee`, but there is no validation to ensure that this fee is greater than zero. If the `protocolFee` is incorrectly set to a very low value or even zero, the protocol could end up providing flash loans without charging an appropriate fee, resulting in potential financial loss.


The code calculates the fee to be charged for the flash loan based on the amount borrowed and the `protocolFee`. However, there is no check to ensure that the fee is actually greater than zero or within a reasonable range.


If the `protocolFee` is accidentally or maliciously set to a value that results in a zero or negligible fee, the protocol could end up offering flash loans at little to no cost, allowing users to exploit this by taking multiple loans without paying the intended fee. This could lead to a loss of revenue for the protocol.


## Proof of Concept

Scenario: The `protocolFe`e is set to zero or an extremely low value (e.g., 0.00000001 WAD).

Execution: A user requests a flash loan using the `flashLoan` or `creditFlashLoan` function.

Impact: The fee calculated is zero or negligible, meaning the user can effectively take out a loan without paying any substantial fee, resulting in a financial loss to the protocol.

```
uint256 fee = wmul(amount, 0); // fee would be zero, allowing the loan without any cost
```
Loss of Revenue: The protocol could lose significant revenue if users exploit the ability to take loans without paying appropriate fees.
Financial Instability: Repeated exploitation of this issue could result in financial instability for the protocol.


## Tools Used
Manual 
## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To mitigate this risk, add a check to ensure that the calculated fee is greater than zero and within an acceptable range before proceeding with the loan:
```
require`fee > 0, "Flashlender: Fee must be greater than zero");
```

This check ensures that the fee is always non-zero and that the protocol earns revenue from every flash loan.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/Flashlender.sol#L97
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/Flashlender.sol#L125


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The flashLoan and creditFlashLoan functions in the Flashlender.sol contract allow users to borrow tokens This lack of validation opens up several potential issues:

Invalid Address Handling: If a user provides an externally owned account (EOA) address or an address of a contract that does not implement the required interface, the flash loan operation will fail when attempting to call the callback function. This could result in the loaned funds being sent to an address that cannot properly handle them, leading to potential loss of funds or a failed transaction.

Callback Failure: If the receiver address does not implement the correct interface, the flash loan callback will fail, and the loaned funds may not be returned as expected. This could cause the transaction to revert, resulting in operational disruptions.

by specifying a receiver address, which is expected to implement the IERC3156FlashBorrower or ICreditFlashBorrower interface, respectively. These interfaces define the required callback functions that must be implemented by the receiver contract to handle the flash loan logic correctly.

However, the current implementation of these functions does not include sufficient validation to ensure that the receiver address is a smart contract that implements the correct interface. 

This lack of validation opens up several potential issues:

Invalid Address Handling: If a user provides an externally owned account (EOA) address or an address of a contract that does not implement the required interface, the flash loan operation will fail when attempting to call the callback function. This could result in the loaned funds being sent to an address that cannot properly handle them, leading to potential loss of funds or a failed transaction.

Callback Failure: If the receiver address does not implement the correct interface, the flash loan callback will fail, and the loaned funds may not be returned as expected. This could cause the transaction to revert, resulting in operational disruptions.

```
// In the flashLoan function
pool.lendCreditAccount(amount, address(receiver));

emit FlashLoan(address(receiver), token, amount, fee);

if (receiver.onFlashLoan(msg.sender, token, amount, fee, data) != CALLBACK_SUCCESS)
    revert Flash__flashLoan_callbackFailed();
```
```
// In the creditFlashLoan function
pool.lendCreditAccount(amount, address(receiver));

emit CreditFlashLoan(address(receiver), amount, fee);

if (receiver.onCreditFlashLoan(msg.sender, amount, fee, data) != CALLBACK_SUCCESS_CREDIT)
    revert Flash__creditFlashLoan_callbackFailed();

````

The flashLoan and creditFlashLoan functions are designed to facilitate flash loans, where a user can borrow tokens and is expected to repay them, along with a fee, within the same transaction. The process involves transferring the loaned amount to the receiver address, which must implement the necessary callback function (onFlashLoan or onCreditFlashLoan) to handle the loan.

After the tokens are sent, the contract expects the receiver to execute its callback function. This callback function must return a specific success code (CALLBACK_SUCCESS or CALLBACK_SUCCESS_CREDIT) to indicate that the loan has been handled correctly.

The vulnerability arises because the contract does not validate whether the receiver is a valid contract address or whether it implements the required interface before attempting to execute the callback function. This can lead to the following issues:

Failure of Flash Loan Transactions: If the receiver address does not implement the correct callback function, the transaction will revert when the contract tries to execute the callback. This could disrupt the normal operations of the protocol and could be exploited to cause denial of service (DoS) attacks.

Loss of Funds: If the receiver address is not a contract, or if it is a contract that cannot handle the loaned tokens, the funds may be transferred to an address that cannot return them. This could lead to the permanent loss of funds from the protocol, especially if the address provided is an EOA.

## Proof of Concept
Scenario: Consider a situation where a user intentionally or unintentionally provides an EOA address or a smart contract address that does not implement the required interface as the receiver.

Setup: The protocolFee is set appropriately, and the flashLoan function is called with an invalid receiver address:

```
address invalidReceiver = 0x123...; // An EOA address or a contract that doesn't implement the required interface
flashLender.flashLoan(IERC3156FlashBorrower(invalidReceiver), address(underlyingToken), 1000 * 10**18, "");
```

Execution: The flash loan operation is initiated, and the flashLoan function attempts to transfer the loaned amount to the receiver and execute the callback.

Result: Since the receiver is either an EOA or a non-compliant contract, the callback function does not exist or fails, causing the transaction to revert. If it doesn't revert but the funds are sent to an address that cannot handle them, the protocol could suffer a loss.


Impact:

Operational Disruption: The protocol could experience frequent transaction failures if users inadvertently provide invalid receiver addresses.
Fund Loss: If the protocol allows funds to be transferred to invalid addresses, there could be a significant loss of assets, undermining the financial stability of the system.


## Tools Used
Manual 

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To address this vulnerability, it is crucial to add checks that ensure the receiver address is a contract and that it correctly implements the required interface before attempting to execute the flash loan. This can be done as follows:

```
require(Address.isContract(address(receiver)), "Flashlender: Receiver must be a contract");
require(receiver.onFlashLoan.selector == CALLBACK_SUCCESS, "Flashlender: Receiver does not implement correct interface");
```

Contract Verification: Use the Address.isContract utility from OpenZeppelin to verify that the receiver is a contract.
Interface Validation: Check that the contract implements the required interface by verifying that the callback function's selector matches the expected value.

This ensures that only valid contracts can receive flash loans and that they are capable of handling the loaned funds correctly. This approach minimizes the risk of fund loss and transaction failure due to invalid addresses.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/PoolV3.sol#L838


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The setAllowed function allows a controller to grant or revoke withdrawal and redemption permissions for specific accounts even when the pool is locked. However, there is no limitation or logging mechanism on who can be added or removed, which could be exploited by a malicious or compromised controller to allow unauthorized accounts to access pool funds during a lock period.


```

function setAllowed(address account, bool status) external controllerOnly {
    _allowed[account] = status;
}
```


Lack of Granular Control: The function allows any controller to add or remove accounts from the _allowed mapping, granting them privileges to withdraw or redeem from the pool even when it is locked. There is no mechanism to limit or monitor these changes, which could be abused.

Potential for Exploitation: A malicious controller could whitelist their own or an accomplice’s address, allowing unauthorized withdrawals or redemptions when the pool is locked, potentially draining the pool’s funds.

Insufficient Auditing: The absence of logging for changes to the _allowed mapping means that such changes could go unnoticed, making it difficult to detect and respond to unauthorized access.


## Proof of Concept
A malicious controller gains access to the contract and uses the setAllowed function to grant themselves withdrawal privileges even when the pool is locked.

The attacker calls setAllowed to add their address to the _allowed mapping.
They then proceed to withdraw or redeem assets from the pool while it is locked, bypassing the intended restrictions.


```
// Malicious controller adds their own address to the allowed list
pool.setAllowed(maliciousAddress, true);

// Attacker then withdraws funds while the pool is locked
pool.withdraw(1000e18, maliciousAddress, maliciousAddress);
```

The attacker successfully withdraws funds from the pool during a lock period, potentially draining significant assets and causing financial loss to the protocol.


Financial Loss: Unauthorized accounts could withdraw or redeem large amounts of assets from the pool during a lock period, leading to significant financial loss for the protocol.
Security Risk: The ability to bypass lock periods undermines the security mechanisms of the pool, making it vulnerable to exploitation.
Operational Risk: The lack of monitoring for changes to the _allowed mapping could result in undetected abuse, further compounding the financial and security risks.

## Tools Used
Manual Review
 
## Recommended Mitigation Steps


Implement Access Control Restrictions: Restrict the use of the setAllowed function to trusted roles and consider adding multi-signature approval for changes to the _allowed mapping.

Add Event Logging: Implement event logging for every change made to the _allowed mapping, ensuring that all modifications are auditable.

Conduct Regular Audits: Regularly audit the _allowed mapping to ensure that no unauthorized accounts have been granted privileges.


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

A malicious user can brick the `StakingLp` contract by donating a minuscule amount of `LpEth` to the contract. It is not unusual for the `StakingLp.Eth` pool to hold no `LpETH` as well as no shares since users will stake them immediately. This will burn their shares and transfer the `LpEth` to the `Silo` contract leaving the pool empty. 

## Proof of Concept: 2024-07-loopfi/src/test/unit

**Prerequisites for an Attack:**

- Empty Pool
- 0 Total Supply

Add the test below to `2024-07-loopfi/src/test/unit/StakingLp.t.sol`:

```solidity
function test_deposit_user1() public {

    vm.startPrank(user2);         // Malicious user aims to brick the contract
    liquidityPool.transfer(address(stakingLpEth), 1e13);
    vm.stopPrank();

    vm.startPrank(user1);
    liquidityPool.approve(address(stakingLpEth), 2 ether);
    vm.expectRevert();
    stakingLpEth.deposit(2 ether , user1);
    vm.stopPrank();

}
```
`Run the Following Command`
```shell
forge test --match-contract StakingLP --match-test test_deposit_user1 -vvvv
```
This attack is possible because the fix for a common donation attack vulnerability was to set a minimum deposit value using _checkMinShares. While this requirement prevents the typical donation attack, it inadvertently introduces another vulnerability. An attacker can exploit this by disrupting the deposit mechanism, effectively bricking the contract.

## Tools Used

- Foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The simplest approach, though it incurs a cost to the protocol, is to deposit the minimum required shares and assets during the protocol's creation, making these values immutable. Alternatively, virtual assets and shares could be used to avoid this cost.

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/4f508781a49ffa53511e7e5ed6cda0ff0eb5bdc5/src/CDPVault.sol#L223-L249
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/4f508781a49ffa53511e7e5ed6cda0ff0eb5bdc5/src/CDPVault.sol#L367-L373


# Vulnerability details

### Impact
Administrator is not able to pause users' withdrawals and deposits as expected.

### Proof of Concept
The CDPVault contract inherits Pausable to provide pausing capabilities to the administrator on users' deposits and withdrawals. The contract correctly exposes the `whenNotPaused()` modifier to the deposit and withdrawal functions. However, these functions are simply used to format input for the `modifyCollateralAndDebt()` public function, which does not implement the `whenNotPaused()` modifier, rendering the pausability feature ineffective.

Add the test below to `2024-07-loopfi/src/test/unit/CDPVault.t.sol`:

```solidity
  function test_PauseAndDeposit_Withdrawal() public {
    CDPVault vault = createCDPVault(token, 150 ether, 10 ether, 1.25 ether, 1.0 ether, 0);
    createGaugeAndSetGauge(address(vault));
    token.mint(address(this), 100 ether);
    token.approve(address(vault), 100 ether);
    address position = address(new PositionOwner(vault));

    vault.pause();  //@auditor Admin pauses contract
    
    vm.expectRevert("Pausable: paused"); // @auditor Foundry Cheatcode to expect a revert only on next line
    vault.deposit(position, 50 ether); // @auditor User makes initial deposit with the deposit function and is reverted as protocol is paused.
    vault.modifyCollateralAndDebt({ // @auditor User bypasses the pause by calling modifyCollateralAndDebt, achieving the same result as deposit without reverting.
        owner: position,
        collateralizer: address(this),
        creditor: address(this),
        deltaCollateral: 50 ether,
        deltaDebt: 0
    });

    vm.expectRevert("Pausable: paused"); // @auditor Foundry Cheatcode to expect a revert only on next line
    vault.withdraw(position, 50 ether); // @auditor User makes initial deposit with the withdraw function and is reverted as protocol is paused.
    vault.modifyCollateralAndDebt({  // @auditor User bypasses the pause by calling modifyCollateralAndDebt, achieving the same result as withdraw without reverting.
        owner: position,
        collateralizer: address(this),
        creditor: address(this),
        deltaCollateral: -50 ether,
        deltaDebt: 0
    });
 }
```
`Run the following command`
```shell
forge test --match-contract CDPVault --match-test test_PauseAndDeposit_Withdrawal -vvv
```
### Tools Used
Foundry

### Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add the `whenNotPaused()` modifier to the `modifyCollateralAndDebt()` function.

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/1b32965bc1ce36b885df687069880140073c6285/src/oracle/BalancerOracle.sol#L9-L12


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The Balancer V2 price feed reads the weights of the Balancer pool during deployment and stores them
as immutable. The oracle also supports managed pools, with getActualSupply(), but from the
Balancer documentation (https://web.archive.org/web/20230928124529/https://docs.balancer.fi/concepts
/pools/managed.html#weights) the weights can be changed by the pool owner. Changing the weights of

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L530-L531


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Detailed description of the impact of this finding.

CDPVault.liquidatePosition() calculates ```deltaDebt``` and ```penalty``` wrongly, as a result, either the position owner or the protocol will lost funds, depending on the value of the parameter ```liquidationPenalty```. Since ```penalty``` will be a small value, we expect that the positoin owner will lost funds since a smaller debt will be repayed. 

## Proof of Concept
Provide direct links to all referenced code in GitHub. Add screenshots, logs, or any other relevant proof that illustrates the concept.

CDPVault.liquidatePosition() allows a liquidator to liquidate an liquidable position:

[https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L509-L574](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L509-L574)

However, it calcualtes the two variables wrongly, mixing one with the other: 

```javascript
 uint256 deltaDebt = wmul(repayAmount, liqConfig_.liquidationPenalty);
        uint256 penalty = wmul(repayAmount, WAD - liqConfig_.liquidationPenalty);
```

The correct way should be the other way around: 
```javascript
 uint256 penalty = wmul(repayAmount, liqConfig_.liquidationPenalty);
        uint256 deltaDebt = wmul(repayAmount, WAD - liqConfig_.liquidationPenalty);
```

The correct way should be the other way around: 
```javascript
 uint256 penalty = wmul(repayAmount, liqConfig_.liquidationPenalty);
        uint256 deltaDebt = wmul(repayAmount, WAD - liqConfig_.liquidationPenalty);
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/PoolV3.sol#L287-L309

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Detailed description of the impact of this finding.

The use of _amountWithFee and _amountWithWithdrawalFee in the withdraw function suggests that fees are being applied in two steps. 

This might lead to confusion regarding whether multiple fees are being applied correctly or if one function is meant to adjust for transaction fees and the other for withdrawal-specific fees. 

This confusion can result in incorrect fee calculations and impact the amount users receive during withdrawals.
## Proof of Concept
Provide direct links to all referenced code in GitHub. Add screenshots, logs, or any other relevant proof that illustrates the concept.

In the withdraw function, the amount to be sent to the user is calculated using two separate functions for fee application:
```sol
uint256 assetsToUser = _amountWithFee(assets);
uint256 assetsSent = _amountWithWithdrawalFee(assetsToUser);
```

The _amountWithFee function currently returns the amount without modification:
```sol
function _amountWithFee(uint256 amount) internal view virtual returns (uint256) {
    return amount;
}
```

The _amountWithWithdrawalFee function applies a fee based on the withdrawFee:
```sol
function _amountWithWithdrawalFee(uint256 amount) internal view returns (uint256) {
    return (amount * PERCENTAGE_FACTOR) / (PERCENTAGE_FACTOR - withdrawFee);
}
```

Given the current implementation of _amountWithFee, it does not alter the amount, leading to redundant operations. 

If _amountWithFee is intended to eventually include a separate fee, the current logic could lead to confusion over the actual fees applied.
## Tools Used
Manual review.
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Clarify Fee Functions: 
Ensure that each function’s purpose is well-documented and their names reflect their specific role in the fee process. 

If _amountWithFee is intended to apply a different type of fee, implement it accordingly; otherwise, consider removing or refactoring it for clarity.

Single Point of Fee Calculation: 
Consider consolidating fee calculations into a single function that clearly documents all fees being applied, making it easier to manage and verify correctness.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/oracle/BalancerOracle.sol#L165-L173


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Detailed description of the impact of this finding.

The BalancerOracle contract incorrectly assumes that the Balancer pool will have exactly three tokens (token0, token1, token2). 

This hardcoded limit can lead to reversion of the _getTokenPrice function for any valid token index beyond 2, causing the update process to fail. 

Consequently, the oracle may be rendered non-functional for pools with more than three tokens, thereby limiting its applicability and potentially leading to inaccurate or stale pricing data in decentralised finance (DeFi) applications reliant on this oracle.

***Use Case***
A similar bug was identified in previous DeFi projects where the assumption of fixed token counts led to systemic failures. 

For example, Uniswap v1 originally assumed a fixed pair of tokens, and subsequent iterations expanded to handle multiple assets dynamically, mitigating these issues.

## Proof of Concept
Provide direct links to all referenced code in GitHub. Add screenshots, logs, or any other relevant proof that illustrates the concept.

1.	Code Snippet:
```sol
    function _getTokenPrice(uint256 index) internal view returns (uint256 price) {
        address token;
        if (index == 0) token = token0;
        else if (index == 1) token = token1;
        else if (index == 2) token = token2;
        else revert BalancerOracle__getTokenPrice_invalidIndex();


        return chainlinkOracle.spot(token);
    }
```

2.	Scenario:
	•	Assume the Balancer pool is configured with four tokens.
	•	The balancerVault.getPoolTokens(poolId) call would return an array of four token addresses.
	•	During the update function execution, _getTokenPrice(3) would be called, resulting in a revert due to the missing condition for index 3.

3.	Execution:
•	The function reverts with BalancerOracle__getTokenPrice_invalidIndex() when accessing a token index of 3 or more.
	•	This limits the pool configurations supported by the oracle and leads to a failure in updating price data.

## Tools Used
Manual review.
## Recommended Mitigation Steps

1.	Dynamic Token Handling:
Modify the BalancerOracle contract to support dynamic token handling using an array or mapping that accommodates any number of tokens retrieved from the pool:
```sol
address[] public tokens;
```

2.	Constructor and Initialisation:
Modify the constructor to initialise the tokens array:
```sol
(address[] memory tokens, , ) = balancerVault.getPoolTokens(poolId);
```

3.	Update the _getTokenPrice Function:
Modify the function to dynamically handle the number of tokens:
```sol
function _getTokenPrice(uint256 index) internal view returns (uint256 price) {
    if (index >= tokens.length) revert BalancerOracle__getTokenPrice_invalidIndex();
    address token = tokens[index];
    return chainlinkOracle.spot(token);
}
```


## Assessed type

Math

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Detailed description of the impact of this finding.

This report addresses a likely bug in the vote() and _vote() functions of the GaugeV3 contract, part of the Gearbox Protocol. 

The issue arises from inadequate validation of user voting power, potentially allowing users to cast more votes than they should, leading to governance manipulation. 

## Proof of Concept
Provide direct links to all referenced code in GitHub. Add screenshots, logs, or any other relevant proof that illustrates the concept.

The vote() function relies on an external voting contract to verify that the caller is authorised to vote, but it does not explicitly check whether the user has sufficient voting power before adding their votes.

Without proper validation within _vote(), users can potentially cast more votes than they have voting power for, assuming that there are no checks elsewhere in the protocol.

The vulnerable lines of code are depicted below.
```sol
    function vote(
        address user,
        uint96 votes,
        bytes calldata extraData
    )
        external
        override
        onlyVoter // U:[GA-02]
    {
        (address token, bool lpSide) = abi.decode(extraData, (address, bool)); // U:[GA-10,11,12]
        _vote({user: user, token: token, votes: votes, lpSide: lpSide}); // U:[GA-10,11,12]
    }

    function _vote(address user, uint96 votes, address token, bool lpSide) internal {
        if (!isTokenAdded(token)) revert TokenNotAllowedException(); // U:[GA-10]


        _checkAndUpdateEpoch(); // U:[GA-11]


        QuotaRateParams storage qp = quotaRateParams[token]; // U:[GA-12]
        UserVotes storage uv = userTokenVotes[user][token];


        if (lpSide) {
            qp.totalVotesLpSide += votes; // U:[GA-12]
            uv.votesLpSide += votes; // U:[GA-12]
        } else {
            qp.totalVotesCaSide += votes; // U:[GA-12]
            uv.votesCaSide += votes; // U:[GA-12]
        }


        emit Vote({user: user, token: token, votes: votes, lpSide: lpSide}); // U:[GA-12]
    }
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Detailed description of the impact of this finding.

The setCreditManager function does not validate the token and vault parameters, which could lead to erroneous or malicious configurations if zero addresses are inadvertently set. 

This can cause downstream errors in other parts of the contract that rely on creditManagers mapping to be correctly initialised.

## Proof of Concept
Provide direct links to all referenced code in GitHub. Add screenshots, logs, or any other relevant proof that illustrates the concept.

The vulnerable function is as follows:
```sol
    function setCreditManager(
        address token,
        address vault
    )
        external
        override
        configuratorOnly // U:[PQK-2]
    {
        creditManagers[token] = vault;
    }
```

The setCreditManager function is intended to map a token to its respective vault (credit manager). 

However, there are no checks to ensure that token and vault are non-zero addresses. 

This lack of validation allows potentially unintended configurations, which can lead to the following issues:

1. Setting Zero Addresses: 
If a zero address is set as a vault, any logic dependent on creditManagers[token] will fail, potentially leading to incorrect calculations or system failures.

2. Incorrect Configuration: 
Mistakenly setting incorrect or null values can disrupt the relationship between tokens and their credit managers, leading to systemic failures in quota management.

***Example Scenario***

Suppose the following call is made in error or maliciously by an insider to the setCreditManager function:
```sol
setCreditManager(address(0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000), address(0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000));
```

This would set the creditManagers mapping for the zero address token to the zero address vault, creating a scenario where other functions, like poolQuotaRevenue, fail or produce incorrect results due to referencing the zero address.

***The result in Remix IDE is as follows:***

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To mitigate this issue, the setCreditManager function should include input validation to ensure that neither the token nor the vault is set to a zero address. Here is a possible implementation:
```sol
function setCreditManager(address token, address vault) external override configuratorOnly {
    require(token != address(0), "Token address cannot be zero");
    require(vault != address(0), "Vault address cannot be zero");
    creditManagers[token] = vault;
}
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L376
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L374-L381


# Vulnerability details

Incorrect permission check in `modifyCollateralAndDebt` function that allows unauthorized modifications to a user's collateral and debt positions. The issue lies in the first condition of the permission checks at the beginning of the function. ([line 376 of CDPVault.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L376)):
```solidity
((deltaDebt > 0 || deltaCollateral < 0) && !hasPermission(owner, msg.sender))
```
The condition is meant to check if the debt is being increased (`deltaDebt > 0`) or the collateral is being decreased (`deltaCollateral < 0`), and revert if the `msg.sender` does not have permission from the position owner.

However, this condition uses the logical OR operator (`||`) instead of the logical AND operator (`&&`). As a result, if either `deltaDebt` is positive (debt is being increased) or `deltaCollateral` is negative (collateral is being decreased), and the caller has permission from the owner, the function will not revert. However, the function should revert when both conditions are met, and the caller does not have permission from the owner.

As a result, an attacker can exploit this flaw to manipulate a position's collateral and debt without the owner's consent by crafting the `deltaDebt` and `deltaCollateral` values to bypass the permission check.

## Impact
Unauthorized increases in debt, leading to undercollateralized positions and increased risk of liquidation.

Unauthorized decreases in collateral, reducing the overall collateralization ratio and potentially triggering cascading liquidations.

The violation is in the permission checks at the beginning of the function: [CDPVault.sol:374-381](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L374-L381)
```solidity
if (
    // position is either more safe than before or msg.sender has the permission from the owner
    ((deltaDebt > 0 || deltaCollateral < 0) && !hasPermission(owner, msg.sender)) ||
    // msg.sender has the permission of the collateralizer to collateralize the position using their cash
    (deltaCollateral > 0 && !hasPermission(collateralizer, msg.sender)) ||
    // msg.sender has the permission of the creditor to use their credit to repay the debt
    (deltaDebt < 0 && !hasPermission(creditor, msg.sender))
) revert CDPVault__modifyCollateralAndDebt_noPermission();
```
According to this condition, the function should revert if either `deltaDebt` is positive (debt is being increased) or `deltaCollateral` is negative (collateral is being decreased), and the caller (`msg.sender`) does not have permission from the owner.

However, the violation occurs when both `deltaDebt` is positive and `deltaCollateral` is negative, but the caller does not have permission from the owner. In this case, the function should revert, but it doesn't.

## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenario:

1. Alice has a position with 100 ETH collateral and 50 ETH debt.
2. Attacker Bob, who does not have permission from Alice, calls `modifyCollateralAndDebt()` with the following parameters:
   * `deltaCollateral` = -10 ETH
   * `deltaDebt` = 1 ETH
4. The permission check in line [376 of CDPVault.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L376) passes because `deltaDebt > 0`, even though Bob does not have Alice's permission.
5. Alice's position is updated to 90 ETH collateral and 51 ETH debt without her consent.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update the permission check in line [376 of CDPVault.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L376) to use the logical AND operator (`&&`) instead of the logical OR operator (`||`):
```solidity
((deltaDebt > 0 && deltaCollateral < 0) && !hasPermission(owner, msg.sender))
```
This ensures that the function will revert if both `deltaDebt` is positive and `deltaCollateral` is negative, and the caller does not have the owner's permission.


## Assessed type

Access Control

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L451-L454


# Vulnerability details

When `deltaDebt` is zero and `deltaCollateral` is negative, the function incorrectly determines that the position is safe, even if the collateral value is insufficient to cover the debt.

The root cause is in the following code block in the `modifyCollateralAndDebt` function: [CDPVault.sol#L451-L454](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L451-L454)
```solidity
if (
    (deltaDebt > 0 || deltaCollateral < 0) &&
    !_isCollateralized(calcTotalDebt(_calcDebt(position)), collateralValue, config.liquidationRatio)
) revert CDPVault__modifyCollateralAndDebt_notSafe();
```
The condition `(deltaDebt > 0 || deltaCollateral < 0)` checks if the debt is increasing or the collateral is decreasing, which would make the position riskier. However, the subsequent check using the `_isCollateralized` function fails to handle the case when `deltaDebt` is zero and `deltaCollateral` is negative.

## Impact
If a position's collateral value falls below the required threshold (debt multiplied by the liquidation ratio), it should be considered unsafe and trigger a revert. However, due to the incorrect safety check, the contract permits the creation of unsafe positions when `deltaDebt` is zero and `deltaCollateral` is negative.

* Users can create positions with insufficient collateral, exposing them to a higher risk of liquidation.
* If many positions become unsafe, it could strain the liquidity of the system, as there may not be enough collateral to cover the outstanding debt.

## Proof of Concept
```solidity
function modifyCollateralAndDebt(
    address owner,
    address collateralizer,
    address creditor,
    int256 deltaCollateral,
    int256 deltaDebt
) public {
    // ...

    if (
        (deltaDebt > 0 || deltaCollateral < 0) && // Insufficient condition
        !_isCollateralized(calcTotalDebt(_calcDebt(position)), collateralValue, config.liquidationRatio)
    ) revert CDPVault__modifyCollateralAndDebt_notSafe();

    // ...
}
```
Consider the following scenario:
```solidity
assert deltaDebt > 0 || deltaCollateral < 0 => collateralValue >= assert_uint256(newDebt * liquidationRatio), "Position became unsafe";
```
See the following values:
```solidity
deltaDebt = 0
deltaCollateral = -1
liquidationRatio = 1000000000000000000
newDebt = 1
collateralValue = 0
```
With these values, the condition `deltaDebt > 0 || deltaCollateral < 0` evaluates to true because `deltaCollateral` is negative (-1). However, the assertion `collateralValue >= assert_uint256(newDebt * liquidationRatio)` fails because:
```solidity
collateralValue = 0
assert_uint256(newDebt * liquidationRatio) = 1 * 1000000000000000000 = 1000000000000000000
```
Since `collateralValue` (0) is less than `assert_uint256(newDebt * liquidationRatio)` (1000000000000000000), the assertion fails, indicating that the position became unsafe.

1. Alice creates a position with an initial collateral value of 10 ETH and a debt of 5000 DAI.
2. The liquidation ratio is set to 150%, meaning the collateral value should always be at least 150% of the debt.
3. Alice calls the `modifyCollateralAndDebt` function with the following parameters:
   * `deltaDebt` = 0
   * `deltaCollateral = -6 ETH

4. The function calculates the new collateral value as 4 ETH (10 ETH - 6 ETH).
5. The safety check condition `(deltaDebt > 0 || deltaCollateral < 0)` evaluates to true because `deltaCollateral` is negative.
6. However, the `_isCollateralized` function incorrectly determines that the position is safe because the collateral value (4 ETH) is greater than the debt (5000 DAI) multiplied by the liquidation ratio (150%).
7. The function allows modification, resulting in an unsafe position with insufficient collateral.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The contract should ensure that the collateral value is sufficient to cover the new debt multiplied by the liquidation ratio, even when `deltaDebt` is zero and `deltaCollateral` is negative.

the `modifyCollateralAndDebt` should be updated to handle the case when `deltaDebt` is zero and `deltaCollateral` is negative. The `_isCollateralized` function should be modified to ensure that the collateral value is always sufficient to cover the debt multiplied by the liquidation ratio, regardless of the values of `deltaDebt` and `deltaCollateral`.

update the [_isCollateralized function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L345-L351) as follows
```solidity
function _isCollateralized(
    uint256 debt,
    uint256 collateralValue,
    uint256 liquidationRatio
) internal pure returns (bool) {
    return collateralValue >= debt * liquidationRatio / WAD;
}
```
By multiplying the debt by the liquidation ratio and dividing by `WAD` (10^18), the function ensures that the collateral value is always compared against the correct threshold.

Additionally, the safety check in the `modifyCollateralAndDebt` function should be updated to use the modified `_isCollateralized` function:
```solidity
if (!_isCollateralized(calcTotalDebt(_calcDebt(position)), collateralValue, config.liquidationRatio)) {
    revert CDPVault__modifyCollateralAndDebt_notSafe();
}
```
This removes the condition `(deltaDebt > 0 || deltaCollateral < 0)` and simply checks if the position is properly collateralized based on the updated `_isCollateralized` function.


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation
