# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L532


# Vulnerability details


The `liquidatePosition()` function in the `CDPVault` contract allows for partial liquidations of positions. However, the current implementation can lead to a situation where partial liquidations block subsequent liquidation attempts, potentially resulting in positions remaining undercollateralized for longer periods than necessary.

The `liquidatePosition()` function calculates the amount of collateral to take based on the repayment amount provided by the liquidator:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L532

```solidity
uint256 takeCollateral = wdiv(repayAmount, discountedPrice);
if (takeCollateral > position.collateral) revert CDPVault__tooHighRepayAmount();
```

This check ensures that the liquidator cannot take more collateral than available in the position. However, it also means that if a partial liquidation occurs, leaving some collateral in the position, subsequent liquidation attempts might fail if they try to liquidate the entire remaining position.

## Impact

- Inefficient liquidation process: Positions may remain undercollateralized for longer periods, increasing the risk of bad debt accumulation.
- Potential for manipulation: Malicious actors could perform small partial liquidations to block larger liquidations. This could be attempted by the owner.

## Proof of Concept

1. Alice's position has 100 units of collateral and 150 units of debt.
2. The position becomes undercollateralized due to price fluctuations.
3. Bob attempts to liquidate the position, but only repays 50 units of debt, taking 33.33 units of collateral (assuming a liquidation discount).
4. Charlie attempts to liquidate the remaining position by repaying 100 units of debt.
5. Charlie's transaction reverts due to the `CDPVault__tooHighRepayAmount()` error, as the calculated `takeCollateral` would be greater than the remaining position collateral.

It is also possible that a decrease in price blocks a liquidations for the same reason. This does not makes sense since the liquidator is getting a better deal than expected. The below mitigation can solve these issues.
## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To address this issue, consider implementing a more flexible liquidation mechanism that allows liquidators to specify both a minimum and maximum repayment amount and a maxPrice. This approach would enable more efficient liquidations and prevent partial liquidations and changes in price from blocking liquidations.




## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blame/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L509


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Liquidation would not be possible for certain amounts and possibly make position go in bad debt

## Proof of Concept
The purpose of liquidation is to remove unhealthy positions especially to try not to let them go in bad debt where the money is impermanently lost.

The issue arise with this simple check:
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blame/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L532
```js
if (takeCollateral > position.collateral) revert CDPVault__tooHighRepayAmount();
```
It is designed to stop liquidating positions where the repay amount is high.
But is some cases especially where the time is of essence, the next time the same position is attempted to be liquidated, their value of collateral can go even lower which eventually would go in bad debt bracket and it will incur loses for the protocol and liquidator when this can be stopped. This should not happen often but it is possible and it can be prevented.

## Tools Used
Manual Review.
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
In [liquidatePosition](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blame/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L532) instead of reverting implement the following code:
```diff
- if (takeCollateral > position.collateral) revert CDPVault__tooHighRepayAmount();
+ if (takeCollateral > position.collateral) {
+       takeCollateral = position.collateral;
+       repayAmount = wmul(takeCollateral, discountedPrice); 
+ }
```





## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blame/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/oracle/BalancerOracle.sol#L53


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Storage of [BalancerOracle](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blame/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/oracle/BalancerOracle.sol#L53) contract might be corruptible during upgrade.

## Proof of Concept
The vulnerability arises from the mismatch in the size of the storage gaps between the following contracts contracts [BalancerOracle](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blame/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/oracle/BalancerOracle.sol#L53), [ChainlinkOracle](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blame/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/oracle/ChainlinkOracle.sol#L32), [PendleLPOracle](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blame/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/oracle/PendleLPOracle.sol#L40).

Inconsistencies in storage layout can lead to challenges in maintenance and future upgrades.  This inconsistency deviates from the common practice observed in the codebase, where storage gaps typically align to a fixed number, often 50 (https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/3.x/upgradeable).

The storage gap in the mentioned contracts we can see here:

[BalancerOracle](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blame/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/oracle/BalancerOracle.sol#L53)
```js
   uint256[47] private __gap;
```
[ChainlinkOracle](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blame/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/oracle/ChainlinkOracle.sol#L32)
```js
    uint256[50] private __gap;
```
[PendleOracle](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blame/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/oracle/PendleLPOracle.sol#L40)
```js
    uint256[50] private __gap;
```

The impact of this inconsistency lies in potential difficulties during code maintenance and upgrades. Inconsistent storage layouts can lead to storage collisions and make the codebase harder to understand and maintain.
The probability of something going wrong with future upgrades is low to medium, and the impact of mistakes would be medium to high.

This is already known vulnerability found on other contests you can check it [here](https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2024-05-midas-judging/issues/30).

## Tools Used
Manual Review.
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Make storage gap in `BalancerOracle` same as in other oracles:
```diff
-    uint256[47] private __gap;
+    uint256[50] private __gap;
```


## Assessed type

Upgradable

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/reward/ChefIncentivesController.sol#L995-L996


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The value of `newAccRewardPerShare` is lower than expected due to loss of precision in calculation.
## Proof of Concept
- Solidity rounds down the result of an integer division, and because of that, it is always recommended to multiply before dividing to avoid that precision loss. In the case of a prior division over multiplication, the final result may face serious precision loss as the first answer would face truncated precision and then multiplied to another integer.
- If we look deeply at the function `_newRewards()` we can see the `newAccRewardPerShare` calculation procedure is presented as: [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/reward/ChefIncentivesController.sol#L995-L996)
```
995            newReward = (rawReward * pool.allocPoint) / _totalAllocPoint;
996            newAccRewardPerShare = (newReward * ACC_REWARD_PRECISION) / lpSupply;
```
- We can see there is a hidden division before a multiplication that makes round down the whole expression. This is bad as the precision loss can be significant,  which leads the value of `newAccRewardPerShare` is lower than expected. Furthermore, the mentioned error will escalate, especially when the `(rawReward * pool.allocPoint)` is bigger but close to the `_totalAllocPoint` value.
## Tools Used
Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider modifying the fee shares calculation to prevent such precision loss and prioritize the multiplication over division:
```diff
995            newReward = (rawReward * pool.allocPoint) / _totalAllocPoint;
--- 996            newAccRewardPerShare = (newReward * ACC_REWARD_PRECISION) / lpSupply;
+++ 996            newAccRewardPerShare = (rawReward * pool.allocPoint * ACC_REWARD_PRECISION) / (_totalAllocPoint * lpSupply);
```


## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/PoolV3.sol#L603-L611


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Precision loss in interest calculations can lead to users losing their accrued interest, especially for users with small deposits when the total assets in the pool are very large. This could result in unfair distribution of interest and potentially cause smaller depositors to receive zero interest, discouraging participation in the protocol.
## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/PoolV3.sol#L603-L611
The vulnerability is present in the supplyRate() function which is susceptible to precision loss when ``totalAssets`` is very large compared to ``baseInterestRate`` ``* totalBorrowed``.:
```solidity
function supplyRate() public view returns (uint256) {
    if (totalAssets == 0) return 0;
    return
        ((baseInterestRate * totalBorrowed) * (PERCENTAGE_FACTOR - withdrawFee)) /
        PERCENTAGE_FACTOR /
        assets;
}
```
- Alice deposits a large amount: 1e36 tokens
- Bob deposits a small amount: 1e18 tokens
- Total borrowed is set to 50% of total assets: 5e35 tokens
``baseInterestRate`` is set to 0.1% per year: ``1e24 (in RAY units)``

Calculate supply rate:
```
supplyRate = (1e24 * 5e35 * 1e4) / 1e4 / 1e36
           = 5e23 / 1e36
           = 0
```
The supply rate rounds down to 0 due to integer division.
Now, when calculating Bob's interest:
```
Interest = (0 * 1e18) / RAY = 0
```
Expected Result: Bob should receive a small but non-zero amount of interest.
Actual Result: Bob receives 0 interest due to precision loss.

## Tools Used
manual code review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement a higher precision factor:

```solidity
uint256 constant HIGHER_PRECISION = 1e36;

function supplyRate() public view returns (uint256) {
    if (totalAssets == 0) return 0;
    return
        (((baseInterestRate * totalBorrowed) * HIGHER_PRECISION / totalAssets) * (PERCENTAGE_FACTOR - withdrawFee)) /
        PERCENTAGE_FACTOR;
}
```

Implement a minimum interest rate to prevent rounding to zero:

```solidity
uint256 constant MINIMUM_INTEREST_RATE = 1; // 1 wei per RAY

function calculateUserInterest(address user) public returns (uint256) {
    uint256 rate = supplyRate();
    uint256 userDeposit = userDeposits[user];
    return Math.max((rate * userDeposit) / RAY, MINIMUM_INTEREST_RATE);
}
```

Consider implementing a dynamic precision adjustment mechanism that scales precision based on the pool's total assets.



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/PoolV3.sol#L603-L611


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Within PoolV3.sol, in the ``supplyRate()`` function, if the ``_totalDebt.borrowed`` amount approaches the ``totalAssets`` value, the interest rate calculation could result in truncation due to division. The ``baseInterestRate`` is in RAY form ``(scaled by 1e27)``, and when it's multiplied by ``_totalDebt.borrowed`` and then divided by ``totalAssets``, it could lead to rounding down to the nearest integer value.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/PoolV3.sol#L603-L611
```solidity
function supplyRate() public view override returns (uint256) {
    uint256 assets = expectedLiquidity();
    uint256 baseInterestRate_ = baseInterestRate();
    if (assets == 0) return baseInterestRate_;
    return
        ((baseInterestRate_ * _totalDebt.borrowed) * (PERCENTAGE_FACTOR - withdrawFee)) /
        PERCENTAGE_FACTOR /
        assets;
}
```
The division by ``PERCENTAGE_FACTOR`` (which is 1e4) and then by assets could result in truncation. However, since this value determines the interest rate paid to depositors, it should be rounded up to ensure users receive at least the correct amount of interest, if not slightly more.

## Tools Used
manual code review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider modifying the calculation to:
```solidity
return
    (((baseInterestRate_ * _totalDebt.borrowed) * (PERCENTAGE_FACTOR - withdrawFee) + PERCENTAGE_FACTOR - 1) /
    PERCENTAGE_FACTOR + assets - 1) /
    assets;
```
Updating the code to this, ensures that the supply rate is always rounded up, preventing users from receiving less interest than they should due to truncation.


## Assessed type

Math

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/Flashlender.sol#L105
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/Flashlender.sol#L133


# Vulnerability details

In the FlashLender contract, the transferFrom() function's return value is not being checked to confirm the success of the token transfer. This is a significant oversight, as the function returns a boolean indicating whether the transfer was successful. 

Some ERC20 tokens do not revert the transaction when a transfer fails; instead, they return false. If these return values are not checked, the contract might incorrectly assume that the transfer was successful, even when it wasn't. This can lead to situations where the contract treats failed transfers as successful ones.


## Impact

This vulnerability allows users to potentially exploit the system by avoiding repayment of their flash loans. If a transfer fails but is still counted as successful by the contract, users could escape their repayment obligations, leading to financial losses for the protocol.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps


Ensure that the return value of all transferFrom() calls is checked to confirm successful transfers. Alternatively, use OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20’s safeTransferFrom() function.


## Assessed type

ERC20

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L140-L144


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Last user will not be able to withdraw `MIN_SHARES`.

## Proof of Concept

In StakingLPEth.sol, users deposit lpETH for slpETH. There is a check in the contract which makes sure that the `totalSupply` is greater than 0 and the totalSupply must be less than the `MIN_SHARES`.

```
    /// @notice ensures a small non-zero amount of shares does not remain, exposing to donation attack
    function _checkMinShares() internal view {
        uint256 _totalSupply = totalSupply();
>       if (_totalSupply > 0 && _totalSupply < MIN_SHARES) revert MinSharesViolation();
    }
```

The MIN_SHARES is set as 0.01 ether. This means that at any point in time, the amount of slpETH must either be 0 or > 0.01 ether.

An attacker can deposit lpETH and withdraw all but 1 wei, leaving 1 wei of slpETH inside the contract when the `totalSupply` is greater than `MIN_SHARES`.

When the last user wants to withdraw their lpETH and burn their slpETH, they cannot do so because the `totalSupply` will be greater than 0. The last user has no choice but to leave the 0.01 slpETH inside the contract.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider using virtual amounts instead of min shares to tackle inflation attacks.

DoS

## Impact

Having liquidation penalty may backfire as it can incur bad debt from undercollaterized (CR>100%) positions.

## Proof of Concept

- Assume collaterization ratio is 125%, and Alice has 100 ETH worth of collateral (100 aETH worth 1 ETH each) and borrows 50 ETH.
- Some time passes and Alice's collateral becomes 55 ETH, which is liquidable (CR=110%)
- Bob wants to repay 50 ETH and get back some extra (maximum of 55 ETH).
- liquidationPenalty is 20%

Bob calls `liquidatePosition()`

- `spotPrice()` is derived. Assume no `liquidationDiscount` 

```
        // load price and calculate discounted price
        uint256 spotPrice_ = spotPrice();
        uint256 discountedPrice = wmul(spotPrice_, liqConfig_.liquidationDiscount);
```

The spot price is now 0.55 ETH per 1 aETH. The `discountedPrice` is 0.55 ETH

The total debt is 50 ETH, and the collateral is worth 55 ETH (100 aETH * 0.55 ETH), so there's no bad debt.

```
        // Enusure that there's no bad debt
        if (calcTotalDebt(debtData) > wmul(position.collateral, spotPrice_)) revert CDPVault__BadDebt();
```

`takeCollateral` is calculated.

```
        uint256 takeCollateral = wdiv(repayAmount, discountedPrice);
        uint256 deltaDebt = wmul(repayAmount, liqConfig_.liquidationPenalty);
        uint256 penalty = wmul(repayAmount, WAD - liqConfig_.liquidationPenalty);
        if (takeCollateral > position.collateral) revert CDPVault__tooHighRepayAmount();
```

`takeCollateral` = 50 ETH * 1e18 / 0.55e18 (no discount at play) = 90.90 ETH, which is greater than 60 ETH (the collateral). This means the liquidator can take 90.90 out of the 100 collateral amount, leaving the borrower with ~9.1 collateral left (9.1 * 0.55) = ~5 ETH value.

`deltaDebt` = 50e18 * 80% = 40e18, `penalty` = 10e18. This means that although the liquidator is taking 90.90 collateral away, he is only paying 40 ETH worth of debt, with the 10 as penalty. `deltaDebt` is 40e18, while `debtData.debt` is 50e18.

```
  } else {
            (newDebt, newCumulativeIndex, profit, position.cumulativeQuotaInterest) = calcDecrease(
                deltaDebt, // delta debt
                debtData.debt,
                debtData.cumulativeIndexNow, // current cumulative base interest index in Ray
                debtData.cumulativeIndexLastUpdate,
                debtData.cumulativeQuotaInterest
            );
        }
```

Before: Alice has 50 ETH DEBT, 55 ETH worth of collateral (100 aETH)
After: Alice has 10 ETH DEBT (only 40 is paid off), 5 ETH worth of collateral (~9.1 aETH). 

This bring Alice into bad debt, although she can perfectly clear her debt before the penalty as her collateral ratio was still >100% at time of liquidation.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider not using the penalty as it may backfire, and all the penalty (profits) will end up paying the bad debt anyways. Simplify the liquidation process.

Context

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The price of the Balancer Oracle will only be updated whenever a transaction (e.g. swap) within the Balancer pool is triggered. Due to the lack of updates, the price provided by Balancer Oracle will not reflect the true value of the assets. This can be observed in `AuraVault::_getAuraSpot`.

Same as the issue described here: https://solodit.xyz/issues/m-13-rely-on-balancer-oracle-which-is-not-updated-frequently-sherlock-notional-notional-git

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Although it is not possible to obtain a price pair that truly reflects the true value of an asset in the real world, the vault should attempt to minimize inaccuracy and slippage as much as possible. This can be done by choosing and using a more accurate Oracle that is updated more frequently instead of using the Balancer Oracle that is infrequently updated.

Chainlink should be used as the primary Oracle for price pair. If a secondary Oracle is needed for a price pair, consider using[Tellor](https://tellor.io/)Oracle instead of Balancer Oracle. Some example of how Chainlink and Tellor works together in a live protocol can be found[here](https://www.liquity.org/blog/price-oracles-in-liquity)

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/4f508781a49ffa53511e7e5ed6cda0ff0eb5bdc5/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L8


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details

From the [loopfi doc](https://docs.loopfi.xyz/the-protocol/lending-passive-eth-yield) about lpETH usage:

```md
When staking lpETH users receive slpETH.

Users do NOT need to do anything but hold slpETH to receive yield.

Yield is not paid directly to slpETH holders; rather, it accumulates within the staking contract, which results in the "value" of slpETH rising over time. Users are able to unstake their slpETH at any time, at which point they receive an amount lpETH reflecting the staked amount plus any increase in value of slpETH from the time the user staked until unstaking.

The amount of slpETH a user will receive when staking lpETH will depend on the current value of slpETH. At launch the value will be 1 slpETH = 1 lpETH, but slpETH is expected to slowly increase in value as protocol yield is transferred into the Staking smart contract.
```

we can know, any lpETH stakers can get slpETH, and the slpETH value will increase over time. 1. Monitor the mempool to watch if the yield to transfer to the stake contract or not.

3. After the slpETH value increased, the users can unstake the slpETH to get more lpETH.

# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details

In the recent Balancer weight and stable pools, use `totalSupply()` function to get the `totalSupply` is wrong because the newer pools have pre-minted BPT, so it would be better to use `getActualSupply` instead of `totalSupply` in this case, you can see the balancer [docs](https://docs.balancer.fi/concepts/advanced/valuing-bpt/valuing-bpt.html#getting-bpt-supply) for more details.

Here is some examples for this issue:

Balancer weETH/ezETH/rswETH: https://etherscan.io/address/0x848a5564158d84b8a8fb68ab5d004fae11619a54#readContract

Balancer ezETH-WETH: https://etherscan.io/address/0x596192bb6e41802428ac943d2f1476c1af25cc0e

From the strategy [doc](https://docs.loopfi.xyz/the-protocol/looping-leveraged-restaking/supported-strategies) we can know rswETH and ezETH is supported by the protocol.

We can see the return value by calling `totalSupply` and `getActualSupply` is different obviously, the `totalSupply` always larger than `getActualSupply`. So the `BalancerOracle#update` always return smaller price then actually.

The `BalancerOracle#update` function called by `CDPVault#spotPrice` finally, so the `CDPVault#borrow/repay/liquidate...` actions can be affected, cause the users `borrow/repay/liquidate` less or more assets.

## Impact

Protocol can account error due to wrong balancer bpt `totalSupply` usage.

## Tools Used

vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Use `getActualSupply()` instead of `totalSupply()`.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/4f508781a49ffa53511e7e5ed6cda0ff0eb5bdc5/src/oracle/BalancerOracle.sol#L114-L135


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability details

Incorrect BPT price calculation as RateProvider's rate are not considered

According to balancer [doc](https://github.com/balancer/docs/blob/663e2f4f2c3eee6f85805e102434629633af92a2/docs/concepts/advanced/valuing-bpt/bpt-as-collateral.md#metastablepools-eg-wsteth-weth), the current stable pool price calculation as following(e.g. wstETH-WETH):

1. Get market price for each constituent token

Get market price of wstETH and WETH in terms of USD, using chainlink oracles.

2. Get RateProvider price for each constituent token

Since wstETH - WETH pool is a MetaStablePool and not a ComposableStablePool, it does not have getTokenRate() function. Therefore, it`s needed to get the RateProvider price manually for wstETH, using the rate providers of the pool. The rate provider will return the wstETH token in terms of stETH.

Note that WETH does not have a rate provider for this pool. In that case, assume a value of 1e18 (it means, market price of WETH won't be divided by any value, and it's used purely in the minPrice formula).

3. Get minimum price

`minPrice = min(marketPriceOfWstETH/WstETHRateProvider.getRate(), marketPriceOfWETH)`

4. Calculates the BPT price

return `minPrice * IRateProvider(poolAddress).getRate()`

So incorrect BPT price calculation can cause users withdraw more/less tokens than actually.

## Impact

Incorrect StablePool BPT price calculation can cause protocol `CDPVault#borrow/repay/liquidate...` actions can be affected, cause the users `borrow/repay/liquidate` less or more assets.

## Tools Used

vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Follow the official balancer doc to calculate the stable pool BPT price correctly.


## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L39


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Two separate functions responsible for converting to shares will cause weird errors

## Proof of Concept
Upon different operations in a pool, we convert assets to shares and then mint those shares to different addresses. The issue is that there is 2 separate implementations used for the conversion to shares which will cause accounting issues. Let's take a look at the first implementation used:
```solidity
 function deposit(
        uint256 assets,
        address receiver
    )
        public
        override(ERC4626, IERC4626)
        whenNotPaused // U:[LP-2A]
        nonReentrant // U:[LP-2B]
        nonZeroAddress(receiver) // U:[LP-5]
        returns (uint256 shares)
    {
        uint256 assetsReceived = _amountMinusFee(assets); // U:[LP-6]
        shares = _convertToShares(assetsReceived); // U:[LP-6]
        _deposit(receiver, assets, assetsReceived, shares); // U:[LP-6]
    }
```
```solidity
function _convertToShares(uint256 assets) internal pure returns (uint256 shares) {
        return assets;
    }
```
Which essentially just returns the assets (removed the comments there). Now, let's take a look at the implementation used in `repayCreditAccount()`:
```solidity
_mint(treasury, convertToShares(profit));
```
As seen, this is a different function. This is the function that is directly on the inherited ERC4626 contract.
```solidity
    function convertToShares(uint256 assets) public view virtual override returns (uint256) {
        return _convertToShares(assets, Math.Rounding.Down);
    }
```
Which calls this one:
```solidity
    function _convertToShares(uint256 assets, Math.Rounding rounding) internal view virtual returns (uint256) {
        return assets.mulDiv(totalSupply() + 10 ** _decimalsOffset(), totalAssets() + 1, rounding);
    }
```
As seen, 2 different implementations are used. `totalAssets()` can even be manipulated by directly sending assets to the contract, that way these 2 implementations return completely different values and cause all kinds of accounting issues.
## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use a single implementation


## Assessed type

title: Dust positions can be left out or unexpected reverts can occur upon liquidations
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L509


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Dust positions can be left out or unexpected reverts can occur upon liquidations

## Proof of Concept
Upon liquidations, we calculate the collateral a user can receive like this:
```solidity
uint256 takeCollateral = wdiv(repayAmount, discountedPrice);
```
Then, we have the following check:
```solidity
if (takeCollateral > position.collateral) revert CDPVault__tooHighRepayAmount();
```
The check disallows users to take out more collateral than the collateral of the position. Of course, every liquidator's goal would be to take all of the collateral of the position. Thus, the first issue is that a lot of unexpected reverts would occur as the `takeCollateral` variable is based on price which is very dynamic. Thus, a user trying to match his `takeCollateral` with the position's collateral can cause a revert.

The second issue is that there are 2 strict equalities that are ideal. Firstly, the one explained above where every user will try to make a strict equality between `takeCollateral` and the position's collateral. This is the one that users would want to match. The other one is this one:
```solidity
        if (deltaDebt == maxRepayment) {
            newDebt = 0;
            newCumulativeIndex = debtData.cumulativeIndexNow;
            profit = debtData.accruedInterest;
            position.cumulativeQuotaInterest = 0;
}     
```
As all values are computed in completely different ways, it is super unlikely that both of those equalities would occur. If `deltaDebt` is not equal to `maxRepayment`, we either cause another unexpected revert (underflow in `calcDecrease()` if deltaDebt > maxRepayment) or leave dust debt for the position. Based on different prices, values for liquidation penalties, liquidation ratios, price discounts and etc., the following scenarios can occur:
1. Revert due to `takeCollateral` being higher than position's collateral
2. Revert due to underflow in `calcDecrease()` if `deltaDebt` > `maxRepayment`
3. Dust position being left out with no collateral anymore, thus no liquidation possible
4. Dust position with some collateral, low incentives
5. Position cleared with some collateral left out
6. And others

All of these scenarios are bad for the protocol and the liquidators. The ideal scenario where the user gets all of the collateral and the position is completely cleared is extremely unlikely.
## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Refactor and simplify the function





## Assessed type

Error

```solidity
function onFlashLoan(address /*initiator*/,....
```

using a simple example 
assume rate is 0.1% ie rate = 10 
bob borrows 10e18 weth via cdp vault hence quotarevenuechange = 10/10000 * 10e18 = 10e14 hence quota revenue in pool = 1e16
alice also borrows 10e18 weth hence quota revenue in pool = 2e16
bob then places another borrow but this time for 995 weth hence quotarevenue change = 10/10000 * 995 = 0 so no revenue is added however bobs debt increases
bob then places this borrow of 995 one more time, both times revenue is not added but his debt increases 
at this point bobs debt is 10000000000000001990

quotarevenue in pool after bobs repay will be (1e16 - 1)
when alice wants to repay here own debt

hence quota revenue in pool will be 1e16 - 1 - 1e16 which would underflow to uint256.max 
this value doesnt fit into uint92 hence a revert would occur and even if it didnt, the value is still to high 

## Tools Used
manual analysis

a check should exist that would revert if debt > 0 and quotarevenuechange = 0

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L532


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

If the liquidation parameters (repayAmount, discountedPrice, etc.) are not correctly validated or if there's a flaw in the calculation of takeCollateral, a malicious actor might exploit this to take more collateral than intended.


## Proof of Concept
In the liquidatePosition function, several parameters and calculations determine how much collateral a liquidator can take, how much debt they need to repay, and how penalties are applied. These include:

1)repayAmount: The amount of debt the liquidator wants to repay.
2)discountedPrice: The price of collateral used during liquidation, which is a discounted value of the spot price.
3)takeCollateral: The amount of collateral that will be transferred to the liquidator based on the repay amount and discounted price.


If the liquidation parameters and calculations are not correctly validated or if there are flaws in these calculations, a malicious actor might exploit these issues to gain more collateral than intended. Here’s how this can happen:


1)Incorrect Calculation of takeCollateral:
The calculation for takeCollateral is derived from:

uint256 takeCollateral = wdiv(repayAmount, discountedPrice);

Here, wdiv is a function that performs a division operation. If the discountedPrice is too low (whether due to incorrect pricing or manipulation), it could result in takeCollateral being disproportionately high.

Example:

Suppose the discountedPrice is calculated as 1, but in reality, it's supposed to be much higher (e.g., 5).
If repayAmount is 100, then:
 
takeCollateral = wdiv(100, 1) = 100

Instead of taking 20 units of collateral (if the discountedPrice was 5), the liquidator ends up with 100 units.


2) Manipulation of repayAmount:

The liquidator might attempt to exploit the system by choosing a repayAmount that maximizes their gain while keeping other parameters within acceptable ranges. If the repayAmount is not properly validated or if there are no checks against unreasonable values, this can be exploited.


3)Validation and Handling of Parameters:

Proper Validation Missing:

If repayAmount is too high, the system might not properly handle or cap this value, leading to excessive collateral being taken.

Example of Exploitation:

If the liquidation function allows repayAmount to be very high without sufficient checks, an attacker might exploit this by repeatedly triggering liquidation with large repayAmount values, extracting more collateral than what’s intended or available.


How This Could Impact the System:
1)Financial Loss-
If a liquidator is able to take more collateral than what they should have based on the repay amount, this could lead to significant financial losses for the system. The system might not recover enough debt, and the excess collateral provided might be higher than what’s warranted.

2)Market Manipulation:

An attacker could manipulate the system to extract more collateral by exploiting flaws in how discountedPrice is calculated or how repayAmount is handled, disrupting the balance and fairness of the liquidation process.



## Recommended Mitigation Steps

1)Rigorous Parameter Validation:
Ensure that all input parameters like repayAmount and discountedPrice are rigorously validated. Implement checks to prevent excessively high values or manipulative inputs.

2)Accurate Pricing and Discounts:
Validate that the discountedPrice reflects the true market conditions and is not subject to manipulation or errors.

3)Capping and Limits:
Implement caps and limits on repayAmount and the maximum amount of collateral that can be taken to prevent excessive liquidation.

4)Comprehensive Testing:
Conduct extensive testing and simulations to ensure that the liquidation process behaves correctly under various scenarios, and that any potential edge cases are handled appropriately.



## Assessed type

Reentrancy

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L526
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L535-L536


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
 Protocol Insolvency:

  - Repeated unauthorized liquidations lead to a significant outflow of 
    collateral from the protocol. As a result, the protocol becomes unable to 
    cover the outstanding debt with the remaining collateral. This insolvency can 
    cause the protocol to collapse, leading to a total loss of user funds and the 
    failure of the entire system.
 
## Proof of Concept
 - [Source Code Line 526](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L526)
- [Source Code Lines 535-536](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L535-L536)


The vulnerability lies in the `liquidatePosition` function of the `CDPVault` contract, where the validation logic for determining whether a position should be liquidated is flawed. 
Specifically, the checks used to assess the safety of a position do not accurately account for the true collateral and debt status. This can result in positions being liquidated even when they have sufficient collateral to cover their debt, leading to unauthorized and unfair loss of user assets.

```solidity
if (calcTotalDebt(debtData) > wmul(position.collateral, spotPrice_)) revert CDPVault__BadDebt();
```
```solidity
if (_isCollateralized(calcTotalDebt(debtData), wmul(position.collateral, spotPrice_), config.liquidationRatio))
            revert CDPVault__liquidatePosition_notUnsafe();

``` 
This improper validation can be exploited by malicious actors to trigger liquidations on otherwise healthy positions, causing significant financial harm to users and potentially leading to the insolvency of the protocol.

### Detailed Step-by-Step Exploit Scenario
#### Initial State

*   **User Position:**
    
    *   The user has a debt of 1000 units.
        
    *   The user has 20 units of collateral.
        
    *   The actual spot price of the collateral is 100 units.
        
*   **Collateral Value:**
    
    *   The total value of the user's collateral is 20 \* 100 = 2000 units.
        
*   The user's position is safe and well-collateralized.
    

#### Step 1: Trigger Liquidation

*   **Action:** The attacker calls the liquidatePosition function with a repay amount that exploits the improper liquidation validation.
    
*   **Condition Check:**
    
    *   The contract checks if the total debt exceeds the collateral value at the current spot price.
 ```solidity
if (calcTotalDebt(debtData) > wmul(position.collateral, spotPrice_)) revert CDPVault__BadDebt();
```   
  
   *   Given:
        
        *   totalDebt = 1000
            
        *   collateral = 20
            
        *   spotPrice = 100
            
        *   collateral value = 20 \* 100 = 2000
            
   *   The condition evaluates to false, allowing the liquidation to proceed.

#### Step 2: Liquidation Process
#### Collateral Taken

- **Calculation of Collateral:**  
    The contract calculates the amount of collateral to take based on the given repay amount and the liquidation discount.

    - Assume the repay amount is 1000 units and the liquidation discount is 10%.
    - The discounted price of the collateral is:  
      `discountedPrice = spotPrice × (1 - liquidationDiscount) = 100 × 0.9 = 90`
    - The amount of collateral to take is:  
      `takeCollateral = repayAmount / discountedPrice = 1000 / 90 ≈ 11.11`

- **Action:**  
    The contract takes approximately 11.11 units of collateral.

#### Debt Repaid

- **Collateral Used to Repay Debt:**  
    The contract uses the collateral taken to repay the debt.

    - The user's debt of 1000 units is repaid using the 11.11 units of collateral valued at the discounted price.

#### Outcome

- **Final Impact:**  
    - The user's position is liquidated, and they lose 11.11 units of their collateral.
    - The liquidation occurs even though the user's position was initially safe and well-collateralized.

 
 
## Tools Used
manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
*   Refine the condition used to determine if a position should be liquidated.
    
*   Consider additional checks to ensure that the position is genuinely unsafe before proceeding with liquidation

* Add a buffer to the collateralization ratio to provide an additional safety margin before triggering liquidation.





## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L419-L425
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L551-L557
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L703-L708


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The incorrect debt calculation in the `calcDecrease` function can lead to improper liquidations and asset loss. Specifically, the formula used to calculate the new cumulative index does not correctly account for partial repayments, leading to inaccurate debt balances. This can result in:

- Positions being incorrectly marked as safe or unsafe.
- Improper liquidations, either failing to liquidate when necessary or 
  liquidating when not required.
- Potential asset loss for both the protocol and its users due to incorrect debt 
  and collateral management.

#### High Severity 
- Incorrect debt calculations can lead to improper liquidations, resulting in 
  direct asset loss for users.
- Valid attack path: The incorrect formula provides a clear and direct path for 
  exploitation, where users' positions be incorrectly liquidated or not 
  liquidated when they should be, leading to financial loss.


## Proof of Concept
[Instance 1](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L419-L425)

[Instance 2](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L551-L557)

[Vulnerable Formula in calcDecrease](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L703-L708)

The `calcDecrease` function uses the following formula to calculate the new cumulative index:
```solidity
newCumulativeIndex =
    (INDEX_PRECISION * cumulativeIndexNow * cumulativeIndexLastUpdate) /
    (INDEX_PRECISION * cumulativeIndexNow -
    (INDEX_PRECISION * profit * cumulativeIndexLastUpdate) / debt);
```
This formula adjusts the cumulative index based on the profit and the debt.
The use of `profit * cumulativeIndexLastUpdate` can introduce inaccuracies, especially in partial repayments.

Let's say: 
- CumulativeIndexNow (CI_Now) = 1.05 (105% in Ray)
- CumulativeIndexLastUpdate (CI_Last) = 1.00 (100% in Ray)
- Profit (P) = 0.01 (1% in Ray)
- Debt (D) = 1,000,000 units
- INDEX_PRECISION (IP) = 10^9

Now, let's walk through how this bug leads to the liquidation and potential loss of collateral.

1. Incorrect Debt Calculation
The problematic current coded formula is:

```plaintext
newCumulativeIndex = (IP * CI_Now * CI_Last) / (IP * CI_Now - (IP * P * CI_Last) / D)

Substitute the example values:

newCumulativeIndex = (10^9 * 1.05 * 1.00) / (10^9 * 1.05 - (10^9 * 0.01 * 1.00) / 1,000,000)

Numerator:

10^9 * 1.05 * 1.00 = 1.05 * 10^9

Denominator:

10^9 * 1.05 - (10^9 * 0.01 * 1.00) / 1,000,000
= 1.05 * 10^9 - 10,000
= 1,050,000,000 - 10,000
= 1,049,990,000

Final Calculation:

newCumulativeIndex = 1.05 * 10^9 / 1,049,990,000 ≈ 1.000009525

2. Comparison of Debt Before and After 

Correct newCumulativeIndex (without bug): 1.05

Incorrect newCumulativeIndex (with bug): 1.000009525

Difference:
1.05 - 1.000009525 = 0.049990475
```

The debt is underestimated by approximately 0.05% in this scenario.


3. Loss in Collateral Due to Liquidation

Let's say: 

Debt: 1,000,000 units
Collateral: 500,000 units valued at $100 each (total $50,000,000)

With the correct calculation, the debt would be fully repaid without liquidation. With the incorrect calculation, liquidation is triggered due to the debt being underestimated.

Amount of Collateral Taken:

Liquidation discount: 10%
```plaintext
collateralTaken = (1,000,000 / (100 * 0.9)) = 11,111 units
```
#### Final Loss:

The user stands to lose $1,111,111 worth of collateral due to unnecessary liquidation, even though their position was safe and well-collateralized.


 

## Tools Used
manual verification

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
 
- correct the formula used to calculate the new cumulative index to ensure it accurately accounts for partial repayments.
- The corrected formula to calculate the new cumulative index is:

```plaintext
 newCumulativeIndex = (INDEX_PRECISION * cumulativeIndexNow * cumulativeIndexLastUpdate) / 
                     (INDEX_PRECISION * cumulativeIndexNow - (INDEX_PRECISION * amountToRepay) / debt);

```
- This formula adjusts the cumulative index based on the amount repaid `(amountToRepay)` and the total debt.
- It directly accounts for the repayment amount, making it more intuitive and potentially more accurate.









## Assessed type

Math

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L141-L144
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L71
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L112


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The last user that tries to cooldown/withdraw his share will not be able to withdraw the full deposited amount.

## Proof of Concept

The `StakingLpEth` contract implements a check for minimum shares to ensure that inflation attacks cannot happen:

```solidity
    function _checkMinShares() internal view {
        uint256 _totalSupply = totalSupply();
        if (_totalSupply > 0 && _totalSupply < MIN_SHARES) revert MinSharesViolation();
    }
```

The `_checkMinShares` function is called on every deposit/withdrawal to ensure that `_totalSupply` does not become less than `MIN_SHARES`:

```solidity
    function _deposit(address caller, address receiver, uint256 assets, uint256 shares) internal override nonReentrant {
        super._deposit(caller, receiver, assets, shares);
        _checkMinShares();
    }

    /**
     * @dev Withdraw/redeem common workflow.
     * @param caller tx sender
     * @param receiver where to send assets
     * @param _owner where to burn shares from
     * @param assets asset amount to transfer out
     * @param shares shares to burn
     */
    function _withdraw(
        address caller,
        address receiver,
        address _owner,
        uint256 assets,
        uint256 shares
    ) internal override nonReentrant {
        super._withdraw(caller, receiver, _owner, assets, shares);
        _checkMinShares();
    }
```

However, this check opens up a griefing oppurtunities for attackers to either make sure that the last user that tries to withdraw will only be able to withdraw (his balance - MIN_SHARES) locking the MIN_SHARES with no way of getting them out or completely DoSing the deposit/mint functionality of the vault.

## Exploitation Scenarios

### Locking funds for the last user that withdraws/cooldowns:

1. User1 mints `1e18` shares.
2. Attacker sees that and backruns him minting only 1 wei shares.
3. User1 tries to cooldown/withdraw all of his shares. However after `super._withdraw` function executes the new `_totalSupply` will be equal to 1 which is less than `MIN_SHARES`, which will make `_checkMinShares` function revert.
4. User2 comes and mints 1e18 shares.
5. Now that User2 deposited User1 will be able to withdraw his shares.
6. The cycle repeats of every new user waiting for the next one to deposit in order to withdraw/cooldown full amount, until the last one which will not be able to withdraw full amount leaving `MIN_SHARES` amount stuck.

### DoS of deposit/mint functionality:

The contract calculates the share the same way as every `ERC4626` contract:

```solidity
    function _convertToShares(uint256 assets, Math.Rounding rounding) internal view virtual returns (uint256) {
        return assets.mulDiv(totalSupply() + 10 ** _decimalsOffset(), totalAssets() + 1, rounding);
    }
```

Since `decimalsOffset() == 0` and `totalAssets()` will equal to the balance of `lpEth` in the contract.

The calculation will be:

$$ f(share) = (lpEth * totalSupply + 1) / (totalLpEth() + 1) $$

1. Right after deployment the attacker will transfer 0.01 lpEth to the contract without minting any shares
2. Suppose the next user wants to deposit 1000 lpEth, which is quite a large amount
3. His shares will be calculated as:
 $$ (1000e18 * 0 + 1) / (0.01e18 + 1) = 100 000 $$
 which is less than `MIN_SHARES`, which ultimately makes the function revert.

The user will have to deposit `100_000_000_000_000` lpEth in order to pass the minimum shares requirement.

Paste the [Coded PoCs](https://gist.github.com/kostadin-m/80660197b371ac5b9e510117a2d49b18) inside of `StakingLp.t.sol`

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider funding the contract in the deployement script and remove the `MIN_SHARES` check to ensure that no DoS or locking of funds is possible.



## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L155
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L174


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Complete DoS of StakingLpEth contract.

## Proof of Concept
Users deposit `lpEth` to `StakingLpEth` contract to get share by invoking public `deposit` or `mint` functions. Let’s see how the shares are being calculated:

```solidity
    function _convertToShares(uint256 assets, Math.Rounding rounding) internal view virtual returns (uint256) {
        return assets.mulDiv(totalSupply() + 10 ** _decimalsOffset(), totalAssets() + 1, rounding);
    }
```

Since `decimalsOffset() == 0` and `totalAssets()` will equal to the balance of `lpEth` in the contract.

The calculation will be:

$$ f(share) = (lpEth \ast totalSupply) / (totalLpEth() + 1) $$

The contract also employs a `MIN_SHARE = 0.01 ether` to ensure that no inflation attacks are possible.

However an attacker can take advantage of the min shares checks and DoS the whole contract:

1. Right after deployment the attacker will transfer a minumum of `MIN_SHARES` to the contract without minting any shares
2. Suppose the next user wants to deposit 1000 ether, which is quite a large amount
3. His shares will be calculated as:
 $$ f(share) = (1000e18 \ast 0 + 1) / (0.01e18 + 1) = 100 000 $$
 which is less than `MIN_SHARES`, which ultimately makes the function revert

## Tools Used
Manual Analysis

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider funding the contract upon deployment to make sure this will not be possible.


## Assessed type

DoS

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/vendor/AuraVault.sol#L199


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `AuraVault.sol` contract is vulnerable to a first depositor inflation attack, where an attacker can manipulate the deposit and share issuance process. This results in victims receiving negligible or zero shares for their deposits, allowing the attacker to claim all deposited funds for themselves

## Proof of Concept
Given that `AuraVault.sol` lacks protections against inflation attacks, an attacker can manipulate share and asset calculations to effectively steal funds from users.
- Attacker back-runs the transaction of the `AuraVault` pool creation.
- Attacker mints for themself one share: deposit(1). Thus, `totalAsset()==1`, `totalSupply()==1`.
- Attacker front-runs the deposit of the victim who wants to deposit `200 ETH` (`200e18`).
- Attacker inflates the denominator right in front of the victim: `asset.transfer(200e18)`.
- Now `totalAsset()==200e18 + 1`, `totalSupply()==1`.
- Next, the victim's tx takes place. The victim gets 1 * 200e18 / (200e18 + 1) == 0 shares. The victim gets zero shares.
- Attacker burns their share and gets all the money.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider either of these options:
- Consider seeding the pools during deployment. This needs to be done in the deployment transactions to avoiding front-running attacks. The amount needs to be high enough to reduce the rounding error.
- Consider sending first 1000 wei of shares to the zero address. This will significantly increase the cost of the attack by forcing an attacker to pay 1000 times of the share price they want to set. For a well-intended user, 1000 wei of shares is a negligible amount that won't diminish their share significantly.
- Implement the concept of [virtual shares, similar to the ERC4626 OZ contract](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC20/extensions/ERC4626.sol#L30-L37). [More info about this concept here](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/erc4626#defending_with_a_virtual_offset).


## Assessed type

ERC4626

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L223
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L239
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L509
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L579


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
By front-running any collateral allocation or position closure of a legitimate user that became under-collateralized during the paused state, a liquidator can unfairly liquidate user positions and collect liquidation profit as soon as the protocol is unpaused. This results in a loss of funds for the user.
Additionally, upon unpausing, it is unlikely that any human users will be able to secure their positions before MEV or liquidation bots capture the available profit. Consequently, the loss is almost certain.

## Proof of Concept
The `CDPVault.sol` can pause certain functions like:
- [deposit()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L223)
- [withdraw()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L239)
- [liquidatePosition()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L509)
- [liquidatePositionBadDebt()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L579)

However, there is a risk that when these functions are unpaused, liquidators could front-run and liquidate user positions before those users have a chance to stabilize their positions.
Note that the repay function is not pausable, but this may not be ideal, as users might have locked the borrowed tokens in another protocol and are unable to redeem them at the moment.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider adding a grace period after unpausing during which liquidation remains blocked to allow users to avoid unfair liquidation by closing their positions or allocating additional collateral. The protocol team can also think of any other way which mitigates the unfair liquidations of users.


## Assessed type

MEV

title: A donation attack in `StakingLPEth` causes the number of assets corresponding to `MIN_SHARES` to be magnified
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L141


# Vulnerability details


## Impact

A donation attack causes `MIN_SHARES` to correspond to a large asset amount, leaving the user unable to stake.

## Proof of Concept

You need to check `MIN_SHARES` in the `StakingLPEth`:

```solidity
    uint256 private constant MIN_SHARES = 0.01 ether;
    function _checkMinShares() internal view {
        uint256 _totalSupply = totalSupply();
        if (_totalSupply > 0 && _totalSupply < MIN_SHARES) revert MinSharesViolation();
    }
    
    function _deposit(address caller, address receiver, uint256 assets, uint256 shares) internal override nonReentrant {
        super._deposit(caller, receiver, assets, shares);
@>      _checkMinShares();
    }
```

But the problem is that the number of assets corresponding to share in `ERC4626` is variable:

If the ratio of share to asset is 1:1, the minimum amount of asset required for `mint/deposit` is 0.01 ETH
If the ratio of share to asset is 1:10, the minimum amount of asset required for `mint/deposit` is 0.1 ETH

An attacker can change the proportion of shares and assets through donations,

When the pool is just initialized,
Suppose the attacker donates 10000 wei, the share/asset becomes ~1:10000, and the share of 0.01 ETH corresponds to ~100 EHT asset.
So other users need 100 ETH to `mint` their token.
Since most users do not have this much ETH, they will not be able to `mint/deposit`.

The attacker does not need `mint/deposit` token, but simply sends the asset to the pool address, so the `totalAsset` value is the value set by the attacker.

Since `_checkMinShares` is after `super._deposit`, `totalSupply` > 0 and `totalSupply` is too small to pass the check, so no one can successfully call `mint/deposit` unless he uses a large amount of asset.

## Tools Used
vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The minimum number of values is limited to using `asset` instead of `share`



## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

## Impact
The administrator function cannot be called.

## Proof of Concept

There are 2 types of permissions defined in AuraVault:

```solidity
bytes32 constant VAULT_ADMIN_ROLE = keccak256("VAULT_ADMIN_ROLE");
bytes32 constant VAULT_CONFIG_ROLE = keccak256("VAULT_CONFIG_ROLE");
```

But the problem is that permissions are not initialized in the constructor:

```solidity
    constructor(
        address rewardPool_,
        address asset_,
        address feed_,
        address auraPriceOracle_,
        uint32 maxClaimerIncentive_,
        uint32 maxLockerIncentive_,
        string memory tokenName_,
        string memory tokenSymbol_
    ) ERC4626(IERC20(asset_)) ERC20(tokenName_, tokenSymbol_) {
        rewardPool = rewardPool_;
        feed = feed_;
        auraPriceOracle = auraPriceOracle_;
        maxClaimerIncentive = maxClaimerIncentive_;
        maxLockerIncentive = maxLockerIncentive_;
    }
```

Therefore, the administrator function cannot be called.

Set permissions in the constructor

warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/vendor/AuraVault.sol#L175


# Vulnerability details


## Impact
An inflation attack prevents users from getting a share, cause the loss of user funds

## Proof of Concept
`AuraVault` is a standard ERC4626 contract that uses rewardPool's balance as `back asset`:

```solidity
    function totalAssets() public view virtual override(IERC4626, ERC4626) returns (uint256) {
        return IPool(rewardPool).balanceOf(address(this));
    }
```

But the problem is that ERC4626 has a problem with inflation attacks:


pool starts with `totalAssets` `totalSupply` of 0,
An attacker could change the ratio between share and asset by donating, sending `rewardPool` tokens to AuraVault's address.

When another user `mint/deposit`, the user cannot get the share due to downward rounding.

https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/erc4626

> When depositing tokens, the number of shares a user gets is rounded down. This rounding takes away value from the user in favor or the vault (i.e. in favor of all the current share holders). This rounding is often negligible because of the amount at stake. If you deposit 1e9 shares worth of tokens, the rounding will have you lose at most 0.0000001% of your deposit. However if you deposit 10 shares worth of tokens, you could lose 10% of your deposit. Even worse, if you deposit <1 share worth of tokens, then you get 0 shares, and you basically made a donation.

> First the attacker must deposit a small amount of tokens (1 token) and follow up with a donation of 1e5 tokens directly to the vault to move the exchange rate "right". This puts the vault in a state where any deposit smaller than 1e5 would be completely lost to the vault. Given that the attacker is the only share holder (from their donation), the attacker would steal all the tokens deposited.


## Tools Used
vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Defending with a virtual offset: 
https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/erc4626#defending_with_a_virtual_offset


## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L141


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Attackers steal other users' tokens

## Proof of Concept

`StakingLPEth` is an `ERC4626` contract with a `MIN_SHARES` check added to `ERC4626`, but this does not protect against an inflation attack,

An attacker can donate the asset token in the pool's initial state, then `mint/deposit` 0.01 ETH share, avoid the `MIN_SHARES` check, and conduct a inflation attack.

1. The pool is in the initialization state, and no other user has mint token.
2. The attacker discovers that the victim bob deposits 1 ETH of assets.
3. The attacker uses frontrun to perform the following operations:
    3.1 The attacker donated an asset token of 100 wei to inflate the pool.
    3.2 The attacker mint 0.01 ETH share and skip the check of `MIN_SHARES`, about 1 ETH asset is required.
4. Bob's transaction is executed, at this time, the amount of share is 0.01 ETH, the amount of asset is 1 ETH, and the amount of share bob gets is 0 due to division overflow. share = assets * totalSupply / totalAssets.
5. Since only the attacker has a share at this point, all assets belong to the attacker.
6. The `MIN_SHARES` check allows `_totalSupply = 0`, so the attacker can withdraw all the assets.

The quantities used above are estimates.
About the erc4626 inflation attack: https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/erc4626

## Tools Used
vscode

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Defending with a virtual offset: 
https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/erc4626#defending_with_a_virtual_offset


## Assessed type

ERC4626

raw_row.title: Inconsistent bad debt check between liquidatePosition() and liquidatePositionBadDebt()

title: Inconsistent bad debt check between liquidatePosition() and liquidatePositionBadDebt()
warden_comment:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L509-L527
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/CDPVault.sol#L579-L599


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
One position may be liquidated by function liquidatePosition() and function liquidatePositionBadDebt() at the same time. Considering that liquidators need to pay penalty to liquidate position via `liquidatePosition()`. Liquidators may call liquidatePositionBadDebt() to liquidate positions to avoid the penalty if the below condition matches.

## Proof of Concept
In liquidatePosition(), bad debt's definition is `calcTotalDebt(debtData) > wmul(position.collateral, spotPrice_)`.
In liquidatePositionBadDebt(), bad debt's definition is `calcTotalDebt(debtData) > wmul(position.collateral, discountedPrice)`.
The inconsistence will cause that one position can be taken as not bad debt in 
liquidatePosition() and be taken as bad debt in liquidatePositionBadDebt() if ` collateral * discountedPrice < totalDebt < collateral * spotPrice`.
```javascript
    function liquidatePosition(address owner, uint256 repayAmount) external whenNotPaused {
        ...
        if (calcTotalDebt(debtData) > wmul(position.collateral, spotPrice_)) revert CDPVault__BadDebt();
        ...
}
    function liquidatePositionBadDebt(address owner, uint256 repayAmount) external whenNotPaused {
    ...
    if (calcTotalDebt(debtData) <= wmul(position.collateral, discountedPrice)) revert CDPVault__noBadDebt();
    ...
    }
```


## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Change the bad debt check in liquidatePosition() to match the bad debt check in liquidatePosition().
When the position is unhealthy and there is not bad debt, the position can only be liquidated by liquidatePosition().
When the position is bad debt, the position can only be liquidated by liquidatePositionBadDebt().


## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/StakingLPEth.sol#L141-L144


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In StakingLPEth, malicious user can leave 1 wei in the contract. This will cause the last staker cannot withdraw all shares because of `_checkMinShares()` check. The last staker may need to take almost 0.01 ether loss.

## Proof of Concept
In StakingLPEth, when stakers deposit/withdraw, there is one security check to make sure the contract's share amount cannot be less than `MIN_SHARES` if there is some shares in the contract.
Based on this design, all depositors can withdraw their funds from the contract in normal scenario.
For example:
1. Alice mint 0.01 ether share.
2. Bob mint 0.01 ether share.
3. Alice withdraw 0.01 ether share.
4. Bob withdraw 0.01 ether share.

The problem is that if one malicious user leave 1 share when he withdraw, this will cause the last staker cannot withdraw all funds because of this security check.
For example:
1. Alice mint 0.01 ether share.
2. Bob mint 0.01 ether share.
3. Bob withdraw (0.01 ether - 1) share.
4. Alice cannot withdraw her 0.01 ether share because of `_checkMinShares()` check.
```javascript
    function _checkMinShares() internal view {
        uint256 _totalSupply = totalSupply();
        if (_totalSupply > 0 && _totalSupply < MIN_SHARES) revert MinSharesViolation();
    }
```

## Tools Used
Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The MIN_SHARES aims to prevent the donation attack/inflation attack. Compare with this method, suggest to mint some shares to one dead address by the sponsor when we deploy this contract.


## Assessed type

Error
